Gottlungs. Native to the most fertile grasslands in the Central and Western parts of the Wulpic Empire (wulpus means glory or magnificence), the Gottlungs’ live comfortably, with a weaker constitution than their neighboring counterparts. What they lack in strength, however, they make up for in their lean and agile build; their gait and gestures are very graceful and their minds are extremely sharp and flexible. The Gottlungs are also a fair and understanding race, making them very receptive to everything, from the new to the unusual; thus, they don’t shun useful adoptions, making the Gottlungs great craftsmen, diplomats, merchants, and travelers. Their land is famous, not only for high crop yields, but for its naturally rich veins of coal and metals. This land is surrounded from three sides by seas, rich in fish and thriving aquatic life, giving yield to a bountiful fishing trade, thus there are a lot of seasoned sailors and anglers among the Gottlungs. Covetous eyes surround the Gottlungs’ prosperous lands, forcing them to take up arms against the greedy, warmongering neighbors. Despite this, they typically prefer peaceful negotiations rather than the open fight on a battlefield. While at war though, they have no rival in discipline and organization and their craftsmen make superior weapons. Gottlungs are masters of their light, but impressively strong, swords, and they use a firm row of spearmen armed with long pikes to strike and defend the first blow in a battle.

Slavards. The harsh North is home for the Slavards. Their tribes dwell in unpassable Northern forests, making their settlements on the banks of rivers, lakes or swamps. They also inhabit Northern sea islands and fjords. These are tall, strong, and tough people with light or red hair and eyes the deep colors of a Northern sky. They are exceptional hunters and anglers; tireless sea wanderers and whalers; fearsome sea brigands, explorers and merchants. Slavards are trueborn warriors, comprising the best part of the Wulpic Emperor’s guard. During battle, the Slavard relies on the devastating power of their battle-axe, which they wield masterfully. Northmen are strong on foot and do not typically favor cavalry. Southern folk tell the tale of that Slavards are so big and tough that no horse can handle such a burden, and so they mostly travel on boats instead of horses.

Khoors. Like a swarm of locusts, these Nomadic tribes move along the Great Steppe at the South and East of the Wulpic Empire. From time to time, they invade the Gottlung’s realm, bringing death and devastation and instilling fear in peaceful farmers and craftsmen. However, when the Great Steppe calms down, the ferocious Khoors turn into average herdsmen, tending their herds throughout their lands. During these times, Khoors visit their neighbors — not as ruthless pillagers, but as tradesmen supplying leather, wool, meat and valuable steeds, in exchange for bread and crafts. Nomads are inseparable from their horses, starting early in their childhood; other races even consider them as a single being. The Khoors, on foot, are exceptional archers — while on horseback, they are lightning fast, with their pike and a light sabre. Mounted on their high-spirited horses, Khoors attack an enemy and encircle their foe, before bombarding them with continuous attacks from each side. Luring their enemy through their tactic of false retreats, the Khoors can wipe out hordes of enemies by enticing them towards their heavy cavalry, and gathering them under the archer’s volleys.

A chill runs down your spine. A strange feeling – as if someone… just walked over your grave. That seems the case on these damn islands. Life... Death… Here, everything disappears, and everything has its end. There are things you can’t take with you when you die: the steam hammer; money, even a whole airship! Everything will turn to dust.

You are racked by an asphyxiating coughing fit. Scarcely getting your breath back, you think ironically that these “Paradise Islands” are definitely going to kill you one day. Sand and celebrium pollen are not the best combination to breathe in.
Suddenly a strange calmness descends on you, and you stop dead, its integrity and wholeness hitting you. Is this the same “Spirit of the Ancients” the natives continually talk about?

Suddenly you hit your little toe. A worn-out boot barely softens the blow, and you hop on one leg, grinding your teeth and furiously thinking that you need to change your shoes soon… tomorrow? No, today you’ll find that sporeboar whose skin you could use as boots!
Without warning you sneeze. What's next? Please let it not be hay fever! With so many different flowers and plants around, you would die before you mowed everything.

You stumble and your foot gives way. Cautiously standing up you understand that you can’t walk normally now. You cannot put any weight on your left leg; it aches unbearably and is already starting to swell.

Ouch! You feel a sudden sting in a soft and private part of your anatomy. You scratch furiously and curse all the gods you can think of who created these islands and populated them with such vile insects!
The air you swallowed down with food all at once heads outwards. That was some belch! Even more thunderous than when they fire the cannons!
You feel a terrible itch right in the middle of your back — the very spot your fingernails cannot reach. If someone could only invent a self-scratcher – that would be great!

You yawn with great gusto but quickly clap your hand over your mouth. It is said the spirits on these islands are merely waiting for someone to open their mouth wide, then they fly in and consume the soul of the unlucky person. It’s a superstition of course, but… phish, best not to find out!

Suddenly you feel a pain in your stomach. You clench your jaws. There are beads of sweat on your face. Perhaps it could be stopped by some sort of potion or ground pearls… You'd surely feel better in an instant!
You are overcome by hiccups. You would drink water, but in such heat you need to save it. Well, try holding your breath….hic!

Suddenly you feel a strange hollow in your chest. If only you could be back in your home country now… It used to be so much fun! Those feasts we held were simply magnificent! And studying in the Imperial Academy! Oh, those were the days!

You lose balance and start to wave your arms like an injured turkey. Your leg slips on something and you fall onto your back. You feel a dull pain in the bruised back of your head you think that yes... if anything it is high time to have a little rest and lie down for a while.

You snort spitefully. A memory suddenly comes back to you of when, during your student days those dirty pigs of quartermasters got drunk and decided that they could make some obscene jokes about your mother. You had no choice but to send your fist right into the fattest one's mug. He immediately shut up and then came back to apologize…

All at once a chill runs across your shoulders. As if someone evil was behind you. You turn around, no one is here. At the wrong time you remember the story of Sergeant MсСalister who died on these islands. He was given a proper burial, but the next night appeared in camp and started moaning and rattling. He ended up biting three others to death. The only way to stop him was to burn his body, which was eventually done. The corpses of those unlucky men together with the cremated Sergeant were then thrown into the ocean. Gods forbid it happen to me!

A trickle of sweat runs down your nose and reaches your lips. Its salty taste reminds you of your childhood when you went with your dad to the thermal waters in Baden… There was rock candy, fireworks and musical boxes with lightning inside…It was such good fun…

You feel your blood rush to your ears and your sight darkening. You seem to notice a shape of a tall and mighty figure right in front of you. The figure is so big that even whilst wearing your jetpack you would never reach its shoulders. What is it? A hallucination or an ethereal figure of some god?
As the sea breeze brings cool air, you huddle into the wind and rub your arms. You wouldn't say no to warmer clothes now, but then what use would they be on these islands…

You rake your hand through your hair salty from sea breeze and shake off grains of sand. The thought comes to you that everyone who lives on these islands are also grains of sand. They live and work, but all it takes is one wave of the hand from some unknown power and… the grain is gone.
You scratch your nose and notice that the skin is peeling off. Clearly your first lot of sunburn is going. But that's alright, the second lot will be warmer and stronger!
An image from the past floats into your mind, a company commander bawling on the parade-ground: “A soldier has to stand before His Majesty chest out, eyes bulging, not muck around like you do!”
There it is again! It seems like someone is watching you.
For a brief moment, you can feel that you are controlled by some unknown powers — as if you were not a master of your own fate, but a mere puppet in someone's skilled hands.

All of a sudden you get a vision of a vaguely familiar face in the air that surrounds you, a face deep in thought. You shake your head and look about yourself in alarm — but no, there is no one there…
You stretch your numb and weary shoulders. You feel like dropping everything, but you're not accustomed to quitting halfway, so you sigh and get back to work.

Suddenly your wrist burns. You jerk your hand back and look to see what has stung you. You notice a wasp among the leaves…there’s the pest! Well, it’s good it’s only a wasp and not a celebrium hornet - your wrist will hurt and then the pain will go away, but at least your hand won’t fall off…
You feel an unpleasant tingling in your neck. It’s as if ants have climbed on to the scruff of your neck and are biting it. All right now, it’s time to relax.

A giant nut falls straight on to your head. Your head rings and you think that it would have been better if scientists had not discovered the law of gravity. What use is such knowledge if nuts are still going to fall on the heads of decent people?
An orange falls on your head and you angrily punch the tree trunk. This has no impact on the tree, but the rough bark scrapes your knuckles raw.

Something pricks your hand. What could it be? You see a long gray splinter underneath your skin. You won't be able to get it out at once — you shall have to bear with it for a while and work with more care.
You stroke the orange tree trunk. The gray, slightly rough bark reminds you of the skin of some sort of animal...
You cannot reach the oranges that grow on the upper branches. You hit the tree to shake down the fruit. Only the fruit that fall are creased and cracked, so it’s better to eat them straight away.

You remember that your literature teacher in the academy loved to talk about how beautiful maidens live on the Acribian islands. They ply sea-fearers with the fruit of immortality and kind Ancient gods eat nothing but magical nectar. If only he were here now… let him see the beautiful maidens and kind gods for himself…

You remember how at home the snow stayed on the ground almost until the end of spring and how the frost destroyed a great many trees. Yet on the Acribian islands you almost start to miss the snow and frost.

The sun shines and it makes the golden oranges ripen. Looking at the orange fruit, you remember the apples in the garden at your parents’ home. So ripe and juicy they were that it seemed if you ate them, you would be young forever.

It comes to your mind that one corporal in the regiment went mad. He started to shout that it was forbidden to eat the Acribian oranges, that they had been poisoned with celebrium and if someone were to eat them they would be enslaved by the Ancients. He shouted and shouted until he was sent to the guardroom where he miraculously recovered, all thanks to orange-less ration…
You feel an unpleasant prickling in one of your fingers. You bring your palm to your face: there it is, a splinter. It needs to be taken out before it festers.
You drop a rotten fruit further from the tree. It wouldn’t do for the illness to spread to the healthy fruit.

You suddenly remember how your grandfather used to say "Cut the grass when there's dew on it and harvest hay when it's dry." Obviously he wasn't in the tropics - here it's dry in the morning and rains throughout the day. So much for the so-called "old-age wisdom."
You notice that there is a lot of still green fruit under the tree. You wonder who picked them. The thought of sour oranges makes you wince. Now they will never become juicy and tasty.

You notice a large caterpillar on one of the tree leaves. You suddenly think of just how amazing the ways of nature are — this pitiful worm is born ugly, but rewarded with wings in the next life. Would there be someone else who's lucky enough to undergo the same sort of transformation?
You feel a burning sensation on your neck. You slap your neck with your hand in annoyance and notice a squashed wasp. What a nasty little pest! You cringe as you rub the bite.

You notice one wrinkled and blackened orange and throw it on the ground with disgust, remembering how your mother used to repeat: “Don’t pick or cure a scab; only fire can heal it.” Here on these islands, there’s no need for fire, the sun is enough.
You see one of the oranges has a funny flaw on its skin, like a wrinkled smile. It’s a good sign! Eat such a fruit and things will look up.

The pickaxe hits something with a ringing noise and you stop. Is something glistening in the ground or are your eyes playing tricks on you? What if it's a golden nugget? Or a bronze helmet adorned with gems that belonged to an ancient priest? If you were to sell it, you could forget about work! You strike again and see a huge rock. Oh well, better luck next time.

The pickaxe hits the ground. You seem to hear a muffled rumble somewhere in the depths. Could that be lime cavities? It is said that once a whole farm was swallowed up by the earth! And for a long time the grunting of sporeboars was heard from the pit. In that case it would not be bad to have a small airship.

Your lower back feels like it's breaking — you have pains and aches in your arms and hands. You want to fall to the ground and never get up from it, but what would the sergeant say? “Don’t break your back! Whoever overstrains themselves ends up with twice as much hard work!”

Is it just you, or there are actually some strange sparkles in the rock? It could be quartz, which means that there may be rare minerals nearby! You were right — a small but precious stone is now yours.

You catch your breath, admiring the uncanny chipped spot. Whimsical lines form a delicate vegetative pattern. None of those grow on these islands… Could that be an apple tree? Or a lime tree... Feeling nostalgic, you sigh and throw the stone away.

You swing the pickaxe with force, but the hard rock suddenly resists you. The pickaxe gives a jolt and slaps your hands. You hear a cracking sound. There is a jagged crack that meanders its way up through the handle — the wood has proven too weak for your efforts. Well-well.
The pickaxe feels like an extension of your body, and you resiliently dig your way in. The most important thing here is to establish a rhythm and then even the toughest rock will not stop you.

The pickaxe enters the soft ground smoothly; like a knife through butter. But, alas, your joy is premature — your instrument gets stuck, as if caught in a vice. You give it a jerk, and another one...Got it! With a nasty smack the earth gives away and grudgingly lets the instrument go.

You give the pickaxe a wide swing and plunge it into the ground — but it hits a rock! You hear a sharp, metallic clang, and suddenly you're seeing stars right before your eyes! Well, even a sporeboar would have been knocked out from such a blow from a pickaxe handle!

You stop to catch your breath and study the excavated soil. It looks amazingly similar to a Sunday pie. There’s the thick crust and here the apple filling. Dad told you once that the underground people cooked earth pies… Ah… Sundays back there at the family home… Enough rest – back to work!

There's an unpleasant stinging sensation in your palm. You examine your left hand and you see blisters that have formed on the rough ridges of your palm. Some of them have burst. You spit, then tear a piece of cloth off your sleeve and bandage your palm. That'll do for now.

You swing your pickaxe and suddenly feel a resemblance to a none-too-bright bird — one that had never managed to learn to fly and awkwardly flaps its wings in its pathetic attempts to become airborne. You seem to feel short of breath — you might want to catch a breather.

You feel as though you have caught the rhythm of Mother Earth herself. You hit with your pickaxe, and it answers with a muffled thud. The rhythm of this laborious underground music seems to reverberate through your entire body, which also feels like it's ringing. Heave-ho, heave-ho... Suddenly, a piece of rock ricochets, scratching your cheek. A high price to punish your overconfidence.

You contemplate the hardships of a miner's labor; it must be hard to dig right in front of you. What if you have to dig down in a mine? Narrow passages and tunnels, groundwater, while a sack of rocks is nearly breaking your back.

You get the notion that it would be nice to build an entire city underground... There would be streets, squares, roads, electric lighting, with steam motorbikes and steam engines going along the roads. Then you look at your calluses from the pickaxe… No, let dreams about underground cities remain dreams.

You notice a reddish vein deep in the rock. This is how they find gold — right next to the copper! You hit away with your pickaxe, only to realize you were wrong. It was a mere waste of time and effort.
The pickaxe strikes sparks and a host of small pebbles out of the rock you hit. Your hand jerks toward your right eye — one of the pebbles hit you squarely in the eye.

You remember an old man who you traveled with on a train. He entertained you by telling you scary stories about miners the whole journey: “Have you heard this one? There was this man once who kept digging the earth until he finally fell through right into the kingdom of the underground god! Nah, of course you haven't. You're too young to know it. Ah well... you just wait until you work in the mines like I have!” He must have had second sight!

Your father used to tell you stories about mysterious magical beings living in such hills. They have few children, so they often steal naughty girls and boys and take them into their underground kingdom. Back in the days you were terrified at the thought of falling inside a hill…But now you dig further and further into the ground searching for minerals.

Sometimes you find yourself thinking that it may be cozier underground. It is cooler there, with no heady smell of celebrium, no sporeboars… What if you dug out a burrow for yourself? It would be great, of course, only all food still remains above ground…"If" is a big word as they say!

One strike! And then another! Hm, the rock doesn’t give way. A thought comes to your mind: how good it would be to have a pickaxe made out of arcanium… but who would give that much for a pickaxe? It would be worth more than its weight in gold.
Out of the earth comes the humid smell of roots, old leaves and sweet, juicy sprouts. You smile, well, it’s not the smell of the woods at home, but still… it’s the smell of life.
Deep in thought, you straighten your back and knead a ball of earth in your hands. It is cold and dry. It crumbles in your hands filling the air with a sweet aroma of celebrium.

You straighten your back, feeling a dull pain in its lower part. Your hands are still clenching the handle of your spade, but you freeze, struck by the thought that Mother Earth doesn't only feed you — she also takes things away. She provides you with food, but also makes you weak. And someday she will take you away, too.
You see a mole cricket and cut it in two with your spade. What a pesky animal! It's small, but will eat tons if you don't stop it.

You pummel away at the soil. With each strike the spade grinds into the earth — its wounds glisten with moisture and vapors as if they were bleeding. Although you have a spade instead of a shiny sword, you pretend to be a mighty warrior who knows no defeat. May the stronger opponent win!

Yet again, the spade won’t go into the ground. Maybe it's blunt already, or the weather turned bad. Now, what's the problem this time? Has the orange tree grown roots? It won't bear fruit, but the roots are spreading. Such a pain in the neck! Better cut it down. Show no mercy! You're sick and tired of it.

You feel the spade give a jerk in your hands. There is a short clang and a sudden cracking sound. You pull the spade out of the soil and see that your worst suspicions were true — the handle got broken at the very head.

A burning pain in your thigh makes you wail and you throw the spade aside. You hop on one leg and see a walnut centipede mincing into the wild grass. Oh how you'd love to catch up with it and kill it with your spade! But the pesky insect has so many legs, while you've got only one - at least for the next few hours. Still, it could have been worse. You're lucky it was just your leg.

Working with a spade is a good way to clear your mind. You start to wonder how many horrid creatures hide underground! All those worms, beetles, maggots and whatnot. All surrounded by the white fat weed roots. It is said that they help stomach ache. Maybe you should put it to the test and eat some junk?

You imagine that there is treasure buried somewhere on these islands. Thinking about it makes this hard monotonous work somewhat easier. You can hear pebbles hitting the metal and imagine it to be a lid of a heavy chest. “The Digger's Adventures on the Treasure Islands” – that's a nifty name for a book, eh?

You stretch to wipe sweat off your forehead and see a mockingbird taking off. After a minute or so, its nasty loud laughter breaks out somewhere nearby. You think to yourself: oh yes, very funny! You've been digging in the heat for two hours in a row. Of course, go ahead, laugh away!

You feel an ache in your lower back. You try to straighten, but can barely manage it. You feel as if someone had stuck a hundred bec de corbins into your back. You remember how your mother would make some sour dough and then wrap it around father like a belt. But you need peace and quiet. You rest on the spade and try to catch your breath.

You see a narrow bright wire crawl past you. A snake! You stay motionless until the dangerous reptile crawls away. You wipe cold sweat from your forehead and thank the gods — this time you were lucky.

You step on a dry puffball that explodes, filling the air with an acrid cloud that makes your eyes water. The spade you drop smacks into your knee, overturning and dumping its load of dirt right into your shoes. There isn't anyone nearby you can kill, but if there were...

Your spade clinks into something with a muffled sound, so you bend over and paw around in the dirt until you find a flat, dull yellow disc with a pattern carved into it. It looks like it could be a hairpiece or some sort of large coin. Probably an Acribian artifact... Better just get rid of it.

You think back to the old stories about how your grandfathers fought long campaigns conquering new lands and laying siege to cities. And now look at you: conquering islands for yourself and the Empire... Will anyone tell stories about you?

It strikes you how nice it would be to find buried treasure. But would anyone have ventured anywhere near these accursed islands long enough to leave some? And what good would treasure do you, not to mention money? There's no community and certainly no entertainment to spend it on. Anyway, time to get back to work.
You bury your spade deep into a large crack. It's incredible how fast the earth dries out in this heat. Some irrigation or an aqueduct wouldn't be the worst idea...

Digging by itself isn't that hard. But when it comes to getting rid of trees, there's so much more work to do! You have to burn and chop them down and unearth their roots. A great way to break your back, to be sure!

A sharp gust of wind playfully raises a cloud of dust and tosses some sand into your face. You have a mouthful of grit, your eyes itch and slam shut. You wipe off the tears with the back of your hand.
The pungent scent of an animal drifts through the air. You breathe in deeply and noisily through your nose... There's no confusing the warm, vivacious feeling that comes with that smell.
You rub your eyes — they are still unaccustomed to the half-light inside. There's clearly not enough light which gets in through the open door.
You take a wide step to avoid a pile of manure and trip over a floorboard. You manage to keep your balance and imagine smashing the bloody piece of wood to smithereens as you rub your hurt leg.

You smash right into a beam on the ceiling, and an incandescent flame flares up before your eyes. You rub the hurt place forcefully, methodically taking in vain the names of all gods in this world, both old and new, who created these damned islands with all the trees growing on this land!
You decide to catch a breather and put your instrument aside. You look at yourself, thinking you're a right sporeboar. Getting those clothes clean again will be no mean feat.

You like working in the shed. Some turn their noses up at a such job as these since they consider it messy. However, you imagine it to be a manifestation of the cycle of life itself — nothing ever disappears without a trace. Grass and grain transform into manure, which provides nutrition to the next year's grass. An amazing wheel that keeps on turning.

It's such a shame you can't eat manure. That sure would shorten the agricultural cycle! At least it's good fertilizer, otherwise it would be completely useless. They say some people somewhere use it to make houses. But wouldn't the smell be terrible? Maybe it's worth building a workshop with it just to see what it's like.

The manure sticks to your spade. You brush it off and remember what you heard about dried manure-throwing tournaments somewhere in the Empire. It might be fun to set up a tournament like that on the islands, just so long as everyone brings their own manure...
Your nose catches a smell of coal being burned. It's always pleasant and reliable — it means there is a human dwelling nearby, where you can find food and a place to warm up and sleep.
A warm thick steam envelops you. It's so dense it feels like you could stick a bec de corbin right into it.

You notice a gray ball in the corner, but it's too late. The snake suddenly uncoils in a swift strike aimed directly at you. With barely enough time to defend yourself, you manage to dodge its dangerous bite.

Fresh manure is as slippery as ice, if not nearly as hard. That part is nice, at least. You can even lay in it and enjoy a bit of warmth, though you have to get up eventually. Hm, if it dries and falls off on its own, will you even need to wash anything?

You get to business eagerly and productively, completely unprepared for a horrible affront. Your spade slips at some point, and the moist slippery mass hits you right in the face with considerable force. Well, at least no one has seen it!

Your eyes adjust to the shadowy light and you notice something unusual. Bending over, you pick up a shiny, iridescent feather. What kind of bird could have left it there? And what does finding it mean for you? The feather is gorgeous, probably from a bluebird. At least, you'd like to think so.

You look up to see a gray blob in the corner of the ceiling. Just before you jab it with your spade, however, you realize: it's a wasp nest! Probably better to just steer clear of it for now... Later, when you have oil and a torch, you can burn the nasty little buggers out.

A little while ago you hung your old shoes on some branches to dry the mold out of them, but when you went back for them you found that some parrots had already made them into nests. Now you'll have to wait until their eggs hatch. Would your mom think they were a good sign or a bad one?

You stop for a moment and listen to the ceaseless bustle of animal habitation. The wood creaks under gusts of wind and footsteps. The birds tweet sleepily. Something rustles, someone breathes, and the delicate aroma of hay is everywhere…
You look around you and think it would be nice to bring some twigs for the animals — fresh leaves and bark are always good for them.

This is the umpteenth day it's felt like someone's watching you from behind your back, though you haven't once actually seen anyone. Maybe it would be a good idea to attach some kind of a mirror to your spade. But what if even then you don't see anyone? How is it that someone as modern and enlightened as you can have such...superstitions on these islands?
You notice that the southern beams gather moisture on them. You sigh — at this rate, mildew and rot are not far behind. You probably need to coat the wood with tar or resin.

You knock on the log and listen. Just as you had thought — the wood bugs have gnawed a bunch of streets and lanes inside it. The wood will eventually rot completely, and the other logs will suffer the same fate! It's like a plague! Would rubbing linen oil all over it do the trick?

The most important thing in this business is how you wield your knife. If it's a bird, you don't have to think much. Chop off the head, and that's it. Larger animals can be tricky. First you need to stun them and then feel for the exact position of the heart. That's where the knife goes. Just make sure it's sharp.
Clothes need mending and equipment needs repairing, so it would be a good idea to set aside some time for that. A little oil, a little polish, some sanding, and maybe even a replacement or two.

You really like your knife. What matters most in your business is have a sharp blade and skillful hands. Neither of those have let you down. With a knife like this, cutting meat will be child's play — it can cut wood like butter!

There's a rumor going around: a farmer saw a bug that looked just like a sporeboar. Only instead of a fat mug with a snout and tusks it had two claws and something weird on the front. People are even saying wild sporeboars can be found in the deepest depths of the forests, though the ones there have two normal legs and a spring under their butt in place of the usual tail and stinger. The ugliness this world has to offer is incredible!

At night you have to be especially careful, since that's when all the monsters out there are strongest. Just take bats: if you see them hanging upside down on your rafters, just burn the whole thing to the ground and find somewhere else to live. They eat everything, and what they don't eat they muck up. They can even grab hold of your hair...

The most important thing to remember when your cattle are healthy and happy is to always say that everything's terrible. Either they just died or they're about to. They're not giving you any manure, they stink, they're completely worthless. Otherwise, you'll pat yourself on the back once or twice and have nobody but yourself to thank for all the problems that come of it. Don't jinx anything!

You remember the horrible pestilence from your childhood, when few owners had any livestock left. The locals used to blame a witch for it, but your school teacher claimed the pestilence was brought by the wind or water.

You glance at the rafters to see a beautifully carved disc with some kind of symbols on it right over the entrance. That type of thing is popular on the Acribos. The locals say you don't have to worry about fog or the Ancients when you have a talisman like that... Whatever that means.
You look at your turkeys and wish they were just a bit plumper. Ah well, they'll still make a fine soup.

Turkey soup is pretty good, of course, and the same goes for sporeboar soup. But the best kind of pottage is made from fat saltwater fish. Those slices of pink flesh, that broth with golden drops of oil — if that isn't food of the gods, I don't know what is!

You think about how nice it would be if one of your neighbors organized a feast. A big ol' sporeboar smoked whole over аn open fire. And, of course, a barrel of beer, because what's a party without beer? They'd invite you. But, wait a second, what if they didn't? Unforgivable!

You clean the knife with a handful of straw and look at the skinned carcass, recalling your dear mother's cooking with a fair bit of nostalgia. No one could cook pork like she did! She would add sour cream and dump in some herbs. The smell would make everyone's mouth water — the whole neighborhood couldn't resist!

You take a swing and strike, but what's the matter with you today? The handle has slipped in you hand, and the blade has sliced off one of your fingers! The cut is not very deep, but it's really annoying!

You recall feasts in the academy where whole mounds of meat would be served. Boiled meat, roast meat, stews and all sorts of fish. And, of course, rivers — nay, whole oceans — of beer. A feast without beer is like a gefreiter without a beard.
You have surely sharpened the blade well! You observe the drop of blood forming on the tip of the finger you touched the blade with. Now, that's what you call sharp!
You pick up the offal and feel something hard inside. You slice the slippery knot with your knife, and pull a small shiny object. You rub it clean and take a closer look…

The animal's body no longer convulses in your hands — your prey has gone limp and quiet. You see the ground absorb the black steaming blood. You feel as if you are watching life itself leave the body.

You are weary and exhausted. The damned animal refuses to let you catch it, making you run around like mad. You feel as though you ran through the whole island. You stop to catch a breath. You are red with fury — you feel like strangling the pesky creature with your own two hands.
Isn't it astonishing — the animal has no idea of the fate that's about to befall it. But then again, do any of us know that about ourselves? Any minute could be our last...
Satisfied, you feel the weight of the fruits of your labor in your hands. You think it would be great to trade at least some of them for things you need. If there were any vendors here, that is...
You recall a tale about someone's turkey laying golden eggs. Wouldn't it be nice to rummage in the hay with your hand and find a few smooth and heavy eggs made of pure gold…

Not a bad haul for today. But just as you're leaving, your foot catches on a board that suddenly pops up out of the floor and you nearly come crashing down like a tree struck by lightning. Thank the gods, you're able to hold onto the load in your hands. You'd have had to start all over again otherwise!
You make sure the sack sits tight under your arm lest you drop it, thinking it would be a good idea to add more salt to your "haul" for long-term storage.
You wipe your hands and think to yourself how nice a glass of beer would taste. Sure, water's important, but when it's all you drink... Sometimes a little variety would be nice!

People trying to give you a helpful hint here and there are the worst! They just stand there and tell you how you aren't digging right, you aren't spreading manure right, you aren't feeding your turkeys right, you aren't picking oranges right. Sometimes you just want to beat them over the head!
You straighten your tired back, but it's a pleasant sort of tiredness. You rub your lower back and inhale the warm and spicy aroma of old hay, feathers, and fermented manure.

There's no way you're getting all your work done. But if you don't do it, it'll just start to pile up. You really should bring over some almond mushrooms, for example, since you hear turkeys love them. But whose birds can you try them on? It would be a shame if anything happened to yours...

You are about to leave. However, since all you think of is how not to drop what you are carrying, you fail to duck in time. The low-hanging lintel seems to strike a whole bunch of sparks out of your forehead. They could probably burn down the entire shed! Your forehead hurts unbearably — a huge lump is beginning to grow there.
As you finish your work, you decide to tithe a portion of it to the local gods. That's only a superstition, of course, but on these islands it's best to just follow all the local superstitions.

Every once in a while one of your turkeys lays an egg. You push the bird off its nest, collect the egg, take it home, and wonder if you should save it or eat it right away. Make an omelet or wrap it in foil? You can't go wrong either way, really.
You leave the workshop burdened more by what's on your mind than by what's in your arms: the old gear for the loom is completely worn down and now you have to make a new one...

Every time you count your turkeys you wonder what would happen if a strange bird ever wandered in. What if it started laying eggs every day? What if its eggs all had two yolks? That's when you realize that you should dye all your birds' heads a specific color. After all, one of them could go running off to the neighbors just as easily!

You sweep off everything that's accumulated on your paths and get ready to leave. But then you start to wonder if you could collect all the turkey feathers, wash them, and make pillows out of them. All you'd need are linen and thread to make the cases, not to mention time. The only question is who would buy hard, prickly pillows like that...

As you carry your load to the exit you start to think about how incredibly unfair the whole thing is. Why does hard work make you nothing but tired, while some kind of inane stupidity or even just doing nothing can lift your spirits and even get you feeling better physically? Is there a way to make all this more beneficial while taking away how fatigued it makes you feel?
You stare into the depths of the water tensely. Is that the dark body of a fish moving close to the surface? Or one of the mysterious creatures living in these parts?

Sometimes you sit there for days staring out at your bobber, having long since stopped hoping you'll go home with a good catch. Other fishermen say you have to have some kind of food on your hook if you want to lure and catch fish, but you can't see the logic. Why not just eat the food yourself so you don't have to go fishing in the first place?

It looks like you have caught something really heavy. You cannot pull your catch out of the water — it feels as though it's a whale at the very least. And this whale seems to be very reluctant to leave its native element. You wade in the water, bend over and try to disentangle your hook from a snag — slimy, but still sturdy enough.

You quickly pull the fish in and drop it on the sand. It actually looks more like a snake with fins, and it's even hissing and snapping its teeth. Still, naturalists can't show fear in the face of the unknown. If you get rid of the head, gills, and the guts, you can eat even the most poisonous fish. And if there are no gills to get rid of, it isn't a fish...

When you were little, you knew that the most famous fisherman in the neighboring village was a beanpole more than six feet tall with long, gangly arms. The one who caught the most fish, however, was a short little bald guy. Still, the former was always the most famous since there was no way the little fellow could prove anything to the contrary. His arms were too short.

Sometimes air bubbles to the surface of the water, and sometimes in the distance it sounds like someone's paddling away, though you can't see a boat. You sit there listening and wondering what could be going on.

You hear a light splash. A fish...probably. Even the fish on the islands are very dangerous, though. Some of them can even drag you back down into the water with them. Still, they're better than water spirits.

The fishing rod gives a light jerk, and you pull it out of the water with ease. What you see on the hook is a mangy little fish that even a cat wouldn't find appetizing — if there were any cats around these parts, that is. You don't want it, either, so you take it off the hook and throw it back in the water.

The cool water looks like it would be perfect for washing away your fatigue, so you happily dip your feet in. It warmly and gently embraces your toes, the waves lightly massaging them with small stones.

When you're near these calm waters, you can truly see how magnificent these islands are. Soft splashes, sparkling ripples on the surface and glittering wave crests seem to connect your soul to the heaven itself.

Wherever there is shallow water in the surrounding areas, you're sure to find leeches. Just wade out into any you come across and you'll walk back out with them latched all over your legs. You could make some real money by collecting them and taking them to the nearest hospital, since they all use leeches. It's just a shame there aren't any hospitals on the island!

The leeches in these parts aren't as bad as the thin brown things you sometimes see writhing around in the water. The fishermen call them horsehair. It's still not clear what exactly is so bad about them, though they certainly are revolting. They can wriggle their way just about anywhere...

You take a step back, ready to cast your line as far as you can, but you slip and fall flat on your back. Damn sea slugs! Good thing you didn't fall on any rocks...your shoulder and elbow hurt as it is. Looks like you'll be confining yourself to more modest casts from now on.

There's nothing worse than tangled fishing line. It's the worst! Of course, you could make a sponge out of it, but the lack of demand for that type of sponge means you're stuck untangling the line. To do so, you have to pull on the sides, even using twigs to get a better angle. You think to yourself: you may not be the best farmer, but you'd make a great spider.

You see circles radiating out in the water. Peering closer, you try to guess if it's a water rat catching fish fry or a ray swimming up from the bottom to see what kind of miser could be using such lousy bait.

You nimbly pull out the line, but your catch doesn't please you — it's but a clump of ill-smelling water vegetation. You irritatedly rip the wet aquatic plants off the hook when you feel a sharp sting — as if you were stung by a wasp. Soon you see a large drop appear on the pricked finger.

You cast the line and think that freshwater fish are fine, of course. But seawater fish are both fatter and sweeter. Just to imagine a sea fish sizzling on the coals, dripping with clear juices… As for freshwater fish, it can have the stale smell of still water. And don't get me started with the fish bones...

You gently pull a large and heavy fish out of the water. The line is vibrating, and the rod is bending till it crackles. But you give it a final jerk, and the fish is on the shore at last, slapping the sand wetly.Now, that's a great catch!

You keep your eyes on the surface of the water, without stirring once — as though you were a stone effigy. Not a single rustle. Not a single movement. All of a sudden, two mockingbirds filled the air with their deafening laughter. It is as if the air itself became filled with reverberations. That's it, then — it will be a while before a fish bites your bait.

You think that walls are good protection from whatever dangers there are on these islands, no doubt. But as you recall the words of one senior leutenant from your regiment: "Walls are nothing - they have neither eyes nor ears. It's the sentries that you should fear!"

The locals seem to have all kinds of superstitions. Some believe in the mysterious Ancients, some in the eternal tree, some in the almighty creator, while others worship spirits of the earth, air, fire and water. As for you, you believe in your own plot of land, the power of reason and new industry.

It may be the age of science, but the people around you still couldn't be any more superstitious or limited in their understanding. They bury coins at the corners of their plots of land, feed wild birds, and bow down to the earth, plants, and cattle. Life is simpler for you: you believe in progress and fortune. Especially when you go around digging up the coins everyone else buries.
You look at the house and recollect the old tradition of hanging the Imperial flag on the wall. They keep evil spirits at bay, or so they say. A flag could come in handy here...
You think to yourself about the customs of the local savages. To make sure their homes stand the test of time, they always sprinkle a little warm blood on the cornerstones. Barbarians...

You think there must be something special about the walls of your home — they suffice for support in any endeavor. When you are home, you are at your strongest, and no wonders of these lands can match the power conferred to you by the walls of your own home.
You think about the warmth of a hearth. Campfires and blazing furnaces can warm the body, but only the hearth in your home can warm the soul.
What else do you need if you have a house of your own? A bright fire in the fireplace and a bowl of porridge with chopped eggs for breakfast. Then, God willing, things will look up!

You think that a home is always much more than just the walls. It is the real heart of a family — a warm living thing. It ties all the roads and paths walked by father and son, grandfather and grandson, into a single knot. This is where all your roads begin and sometimes come to an end.

You're not the best painter out there, so you come up with a novel way to decorate one of the walls in your home: you just write out the words "sun," "sky," "grass," "table," "pot," and "three apples." And voila, your still-life masterpiece is done! But then that "three apples" catches your eyes and you decide to change it to "two apples." Two should be plenty.

Wouldn't it be nice if a spring suddenly appeared on your property? You could set up a washbasin, and maybe even a shower. And what about a geyser? Then you could both wash in hot water and sell medicinal mud. If the volcano woke up, you could even go without firewood when the weather turns cold. To be fair, you could go without everything else too...

Sooner or later you'll have to have some kids so there's someone you can pass everything you've created on to. Sure, they'll put up a fuss and tell you how they want to go live on the mainland, but you'll implore them to stay on the islands. You won't be able to force them to stay though...and, in that case, why do you need them in the first place?
You remember your father, who claimed that even porridge was thicker at home. He was absolutely right — you'll never find such home cooking on these islands!
You remember your mom and realize it's been forever since you last wrote her. She doesn't even know your address! Is she still alive? Yes! Time to get your hands on some paper and a pen!
It strikes you that you love your home just because it is yours — not because of its size or wealth.

It occurs to you that superstitions can make life simpler, since they give people something to trust and something to blame when everything goes wrong. Realists have to accept the world for what it actually is.

Dreaming about palaces and bright houses is all fine and dandy, but all you need after you've lived through tough ordeals is a little corner, a bench to lie on, and a bit of turkey. Or, even better, a whole turkey! And some beer!

Your family is a veritable fount of wisdom. Someone once said that a man's home is his castle. You look around at your own home and note that it still has a ways to go before anyone would call it a castle. There's still work to do!

You air out your home pretty frequently. The smell doesn't bother you (the aroma your food gives off soaks into the ceiling and walls and takes care of that); it's just that the sweltering heat can be overwhelming if you don't.

You notice a hollow in the tree trunk and shudder. It appears to you that it's the hiding place of a poisonous snake. But, luckily, it's no more than a woodpecker's grass-snake. It has the same coloring and head movements, and it's very common on the Acribos. You wonder if it's protecting itself from you or perhaps it's just its way of making fun of you?

You've had your eye on this old tree for a while now. If it weren't so stubborn, you'd have chopped it up for firewood a long time ago. But for now the two of you have agreed to a temporary truce. And sometimes...in the tangle of branches you can just about catch an intent and watchful look.

The trunk bears a mark left long ago by a lightning strike. Fresh bark has gradually closed the wound, but it will always be there to some extent. You too try to forget past troubles, though you know their memory will never leave you.

Standing under this tree is like being in some kind of green tent. All that's missing is some music and ancient druids beginning their rites. You know, it wouldn't hurt if they actually did appear and left some kind of offering. Some good food would be nice!
You prod at a piece of old bark and see fat white maggots of bark beetles underneath. Well, at least they can save a starving person from death.

You notice a grayish fruit partially obscured in the branches and decide to pick it. Could the old tree really have some kind of usefulness in it? But inside the fruit you hear a buzzing followed by an ominous hum. Out pop some wasps. There's the usefulness: time for a nice, invigorating run!
You really do need to be careful with these trees, bushes, and weeds. The greenery could be hiding dangerous and awfully hungry insects. Hm, what could their diet have been before you came along?

It looks like there's a grassy ball hanging on a branch. You look closer and peer inside to see a clutch of small eggs. They might make a nice snack, but what if they're snake eggs? Or, worse, about to hatch?
You step on a hump in the ground next to an ancient root when it suddenly collapses, leaving you knee-deep in an ant colony. Thousands of tiny insects attack your leg. It burns like the dickens!

Trying to maintain your balance, your arm waves around and lands palm-first on a sharp branch. The branch buries itself in your hand and, enraged, you beat the trunk with your other one, only to feel the bark scratch it. Maybe you should leave that particular tree alone...
How old could this giant be? It would be stupid to chop it down only to count its rings, but what about a thick branch? They have rings too, right? Or would they just tell you how old that branch is?

You accidentally break off a branch. The leaves still quiver, but they're already doomed. A drop of sap appears at the broken end. On impulse, you lick it and find that it tastes sweet. For a second you're a kid again, hiding in the bushes from parents angry about some prank you pulled. Ah, you've had some good times in your life!

Something metal glints in the rays of light filtering through the blanket of leaves. You look closer and notice a faded silver chain with a ball of sea resin attached to it hanging on a branch. It's a cheap decoration from a forgotten life.

You look the tree over and realize that the size of its crown must have everything to do with the freedom it had to grow. There's nothing like it anywhere in the vicinity. Still, the trunk is knobby and gnarled. If it had grown in a thick forest, it would have sprouted straighter and even taller. It's interesting how circumstance and form interact with each other...
You look at the tree and realize that, if you skimp, it could yield enough wood to build a whole house. Maybe even more than one. Though you'd need a good tool for that.

There's something about this tree that keeps pulling you back. Maybe one of your ancestors was a druid? Although, to be fair, he could just as well have been a lumberjack. At least, that's the kind of nonsense you'd be thinking if it weren't for your education!

The tree's bark is thick, dark, and somewhat soft. When you were a child, you liked to use bark like that to carve little boats you would float in spring creeks. You stick your hand in your pocket to dig out your penknife and cut your finger on its open blade. Okay, then! That's what you get for mindless daydreaming!

In an attempt to walk all the way around the tree, you carefully push aside a shrub's thorny branches. Suddenly you feel something move under your feet, and at the same time a handle bleached ashen gray by the rain smacks you in the nose. Damn, that stings! Greetings from the past—someone left a rake in the bushes!

If you were still a child, you'd be thrilled to see these thickets, that ancient bark, the knotty roots. You'd happily make up stories about funny gnomes and terrible sorcerers. But no, those times are past, and now you look for edible mushrooms and fallen nuts among the roots rather than those sorcerers.

On the other side of the tree you find claw marks. What kind of beast could have left them up there at eye level? And how are they so even? The marks are old, but you can kiss peaceful sleep goodbye if the creature that left them is still around here...

You notice some wild radishes among the weeds, and in the blink of an eye you're holding several of the large tubers. You're about to head down to the water to wash them, but, on second thought, you just brush them off on your pants and eat them as they are...

Judging by the bees buzzing around, some of the flowers scattered nearby can be used to make honey. Interesting. Is there any way you could cut out the orange-and-black middlemen and make the honey yourself?

You pull up a nondescript weed and are surprised to see that its root looks like a person in mid-stride. You swear you've heard about that kind of plant before, but you can't remember if the root is a strong poison or a laxative...

Once somebody picked up a stick, stood up on their hind legs, made a stone tool, and set off down the path toward enlightenment... You look at the dirt caked on your fingers, your blackened nails, and the calluses thickening your palms, and wonder to yourself if the trajectory of progress can ever be reversed.

You give the little root you found a taste, finding it neither sweet nor bitter. The plant is a bit reticent to reveal its secrets. It sure would be nice to have a guide to the edible plants on Acribo, as that would save you the trouble of waiting to see if you're poisoned every time you try something new.

Hunger makes people do crazy things, so you try your luck and bite into the tasteless root. Your mouth fills with saliva, grains of sand crunch along your teeth. You'd better eat as much as you can: if it's edible, you'll be full. If it isn't, you'll die faster and stop suffering.

You note that hunger makes you...simpler. Ethical considerations go out the window and your choices are reduced to the binary of edible/non-edible. Unfortunately, the only edible meat in the vicinity is you.
You wander around your property and try to recall chapters from your plant-cultivation textbook. Sadly, the only things coming to mind are excerpts from a cookbook...

How do you grow closer to nature if you don't know the names of all the different trees and plants? Maybe you can make up names of your own? That huge oak is a grandfather, the prickly weed is a plague, and orange trees are yellowfruits. Have pity, yellowfruit, and grow an orange or two!

You pull up weeds, one after another, and check to see how their roots taste. Some of them have to be edible. Suddenly your mouth fills with sticky saliva and your tongue starts to burn. You spit and rinse your mouth out with water, making a mental note to leave plants with prickly leaves and blue flowers alone in the future!

Chewing your food is important. Especially when you're eating roots and plants. Your jaw already aches, though you chew away to make sure you don't have a recurrence of that one time where some unchewed food went down the wrong pipe! Any more of that and you'll start mooing like a cow...

You try to pull up a clump of plants, anticipating the taste of their delicious roots as you do, but the tough stems slice through your fingers. Blood mingles with the dirt on your hands and drips onto the ground. You let out a string of curses and quickly pee on the wound in hopes of staving off an infection.
You're gradually learning which kinds of plants have which roots. Now all you have to remember is which roots make you sick, which make your head spin, and which make you see things.

A scary thought hits you: what if you pull up all the plants in sight? What if you end up eating the tender young roots as well as the tough old ones? Most important is to make sure you don't end up eating dirt!

A smart idea makes its way into your head: you should focus on eating what you see other creatures already snacking on. You find some burdoch plants the caterpillars have been eating and give them a try. They turn out to be more than edible, if bitter in spots. But when you turn over a leaf you're in the middle of see that the underside is covered in green caterpillars, your stomach quickly empties its contents onto the ground next to you.

Red worms squirm out of the soil hanging onto the roots you pulled up. You collect them on your palm and wonder what you could do with them. You're not ready to eat them just yet, but if you fried them...

You note that you've started to recognize smells better. Some plants you can even find with your eyes closed, and you freeze like a squirrel whenever you hear anything rustling in the underbrush. It's a good thing there's no fur growing on your arms and legs yet.

It really is a shame that you didn't have a survival course at the academy or in the army. That way you'd know which plants and roots were the most useful and which weren't useful at all. And, damn it all, you'd know which ones you could smoke!

The more plants you stuff into your stomach, the more it growls, and the stewed meat you keep seeing in front of you is getting more and more vivid. You try to grab it, but your fingers clasp around nothing but air. A mirage...

You think about starting a fire... There are plenty of stones around, but all they give you is more pain for your already scraped fingers. Not a single spark. You should probably try rubbing them together...

In any case, you should collect all the stones, if only to make sure you don't trip over them. Who knows, maybe they'll come in handy at some point once they're all in a pile. The main thing is to start by poking them with a stick. That last one hissed, snapped its teeth, and tottered off into the nearest thicket. What doesn't this place have?!

The next stone turns out to be soft and almost white limestone. Suddenly you think back to your years of study... How your natural science teacher made you learn all the minerals... You look around, though there isn't a single blackboard in sight. But who's going to be calling you up to the board anyway?

There's something off about the next little rock. It's giving off a dull yellowish-brownish color...could it really be flint? If you can attach a handle with a piece of sturdy twine, it'll pass for a stone axe!
Modern man isn't equipped to live out in the wild. That thought is gradually growing stronger in your head, something that doesn't cheer you up in the least.

You read somewhere that you can heat stones in a fire and throw them into water to get it to boil. Then you can toss in meat and roots to come up with a decent soup. You have plenty of stones, so all you have left to do is light a fire, find a pot, and collect the roots and meat. That last part will be the hardest of all.

Some of the rocks, the ones with the crystals inside, are actually pretty beautiful. You think to yourself about what would happen if you found a gold nugget in one of them. Nothing, actually, since nobody has any use for gold nuggets on these wild islands...

Your grandmother always used to say that order comes first. You look around to see that the nearby stones have been gathered into one pile, while the weeds you've pulled up have been gathered into another. Soon everything will be just so. As long as you don't die of hunger first.

The next stone turns out to be the size of your head and almost perfectly round. It reminds you of how your grandmother used to pickle different things for winter. She used stones just like this one to weigh down the wooden lids... Ah, for just one of her jars...

It looks you may have been better off sorting the stones rather than heaping them all up in a single pile. Here's another one that looks like flint. If you can find enough of it, you can start a lighter factory...

To test the next stone, you knock it against a piece of limestone and see the latter crumble. Just as you thought: flint! You could probably use it to make some sort of flintlock weapon if that were something you needed...

Your stone mountain is growing, but you still haven't figured out if it's all trash or some kind of valuable ore. At least you're finding more flint. But, then again, what are you going to do with so many flint axes?

The search continues, an odd fervor driving you onward. You pounce on each subsequent rock as if finding rare treasure, gradually dragging them all to your large pile. Excellent! Now you just have to think of what you can use the pile for...

Humankind has spent so many hundreds of years evolving! Steamships ply the oceans! Airships conquer the skies! And on a chunk of land lost in the jungle is one lonely, hungry person trying to survive. You. Not a bad reason to become a philosopher...

Wouldn't it be so much nicer to collect stones on the seashore? There the waves clean them, rub off any jagged edges, polish them, and wash them right up to you. Plus, there are clams you can find and eat.

Your father told you that everything worth doing is worth doing well and meticulously. You look around and happily note that you can't see a single stone on the ground around you. But then you have a scary thought: how many more are there buried in the ground?!

Your mom once told you that rocks with holes in them are called chicken gods. You look down to see just such a rock in your hands, but there isn't much to say... If regular gods can't help people, there isn't much hope for chicken gods.

Once upon a time you visited the capital museum and saw a wonderful vase sculpted out of one large chunk of stone. You're holding a stone just like that one... No, you probably wouldn't be able to make something that delicate... Nothing more than a foundation block, that's all.

There are probably lands off somewhere where there aren't any stones. Instead they have, for example, clay. Or sand, which is even worse. How happy the people there would be to see a rock pile like this one! There are probably even countries without clay or sand that are made of nothing but soil. They must grow so much food the locals don't know what to do with it all. You hop around, yelling at them: "What do you mean, you don't know what to do with it all? Here! Bring it here!"

You missed a vine crossing your path and fell flat on your face. It's a good thing there aren't any rocks around anymore or you might have really gotten hurt. As it is, you can just lie there trying to ignore the pain in your sprained ankle.

Something glinted in the grass. You lean over and pick up a tiny shell to see a piece of rotten twine hanging from a hole drilled in its pearly side. Who could have dropped a piece of jewelry like that? You look around and straighten your trusty pistol in your belt. The natives are no joke...

Your throat is parched. You look up at the sky, but there isn't a cloud in sight. You pause and cock your ears, but you can't hear the gurgle of even a tiny brook. Sooner or later you're going to have to go looking for water...
You've heard that silver purifies water, but you don't have any silver. What if you tossed some other kind of stone into the water instead? Might flint, for example, work just as well as silver?

It's a shame people can't fly like birds. On the other hand, if they could, they wouldn't have arms. Of course, you could give them wings instead of legs, but that would probably make it difficult to fly. Mother Nature isn't that stupid...

You find an old waterskin among your belongings and set off to find water. Happily, the nearest pool isn't that far away, though you decide to first jump in and, in so doing, kick up some silt. It looks like you'll have to wait for it to settle now.

Look at all the fish! The little fry dart around near the surface, while the shadows of their larger friends lurk deeper down. Incidentally, you need clean water more than you need fish... Later on you'll come back to catch a few of them.

A fin big enough to belong to an enormous fish knifes its way out of the water, but you don't have a boat. On the other hand, you do have the ability to run up and down the bank hopping in excitement.
Is it just you or did a water bug get into your waterskin along with the water? Well, all the worse for him. You'll still drink the water, though you'll have to strain it through your teeth.

You gulp down a few mouthfuls and listen cautiously to the rumbling coming from your stomach. It looks like you should have boiled the water first. On the other hand, you do need to harden yourself, and you were so thirsty you couldn't have waited that long.

You decide to walk along the bank looking for a spring with cleaner water. A dozen steps later you're hit by an intelligent thought: there's no need for you to lug around a waterskin full of dirty water.

The water gurgles into the waterskin and you watch a bug doing its best not to get sucked in. Finally it gets away and swims off to the far edge of the water. For some reason it reminds you of yourself.
You find a few smooth stones on the bank and skip them across the surface of the water. The final one skips a grand total of ten times.

The farther you go along the shore, the deeper you're drawn into the mood of the place: the yellow sand, the hot sun, and the waves washing in and out sooth you and leave you feeling almost lyrical. Maybe you should write an ode to this spot?

Finally you come across a spring. The mirror-like surface of the tiny pool quivers among the boulders that line it. You fall on your stomach and drink greedily, thinking that you've never tasted anything more delicious in your life.

Unfortunately, the spring is too small for you to fill your waterskin. Instead, you beat down grass a bit higher, ignoring the burning sensation you get when you touch it, and stick the neck under a thin stream trickling down from a rock.
A waterskin full of cold, clean water, a clear sky over your head, and a sun that isn't quite so hot today... Things are looking up!

You're trying to get back to dry ground when you suddenly hear a hissing near your legs. A sharp pain shoots through your knee. Swamp snake! Their bite isn't deadly, though it's certainly painful and upsetting... You'd better quickly clean the wound and tie off your leg above the knee!

Your dad told you that people can't go more than ten days without water, though they can live for a month and a half without food. Your mom added that people can't live without bread, period. You laughed at her and secretly threw your crusts behind a wardrobe. Now all you want is to find that wardrobe and those crusts of bread.

It's a good thing the spring water is fresh, not like the mineral water they fill bottles with at the Empire's resorts. Although mineral water quenches thirst better, and in this heat you're always looking for a drink.

Washing up in cold water is such a good feeling. Your head clears, the sun stops beating down so harshly, the birds sing more happily... And the hopelessness of life in Acribo comes into crystal-clear focus...

The barely rippling water reflects sedges, trees, and the clouds drifting by overhead. You lean out over the water to see your own face. Not a bad mirror, just a shame you can't take it home with you.

Coming across a fallen tree, you carefully bend back some bark. What a catch! A dozen bark beetle larvae. They say the locals consider them a delicacy, while all of your people who've tried them compare the taste to roasted nuts... How do you feel about trying them?

A sudden gust of wind blows a cloud of yellow pollen down out of the crown of the tree. In a flash, you and your clothes are both yellow and sticky, almost as if you were dipped in some sort of syrup. You lick your fingers to find that the pollen is sweet. Maybe you should stand there a little while longer?
The branch you were clinging to snaps and you fall flat on your back. Ah, well, you think to yourself as you lie there. No pain, no gain...

You pick out a nice, flexible branch and try to break it off, though your hands slip and the branch snaps back, catching you right under the chin. You wake up lying under the tree. There's a ringing in your head. It doesn't look like the tree is that excited about parting with its branches...

You walk around the tree, wondering how you could get your hands on the branches at the top. A twig looks like your ticket up there, but it breaks and skins your hand when you grab it. So far the tree is winning...

You lie down under the tree and look at its trunk and at its crown, which shelters you from the sky, and realize that not all things in this world were made for you to break or even touch. Maybe it's better to let it grow, a treat for the eyes.

You notice some bluish berries on a bush, pluck a handful, and are about to bite down on them when you realize that there's an unbearable burning sensation coming from where the berry juice has gotten on your hand. In a flash, you spit, wash your hands and lips, and shudder to think what would have happened had you swallowed...

At the academy you were told that some caterpillars are naturally covered in bright colors and fuzz to ward off birds. You aren't a bird, however, and so you aren't scared in the least when you see something bright red, the size of your palm, and even with horns crawling on the bark.
You're very well aware that superstitions have no basis in science, but... Some of the things that happen in Acribo... Sometimes it seems like science itself has no basis here...
You break off a chunk of bark and carefully bite into it. Judging by the unbearable bitterness, it should help when you have a fever.
You close your eyes and imagine how nice it would be if your hard work came with a generous reward in the form of coming harvests and offspring for your cattle.

You can't stop wanting to climb up to the top of the tree and get a look around, so you make a crazy attempt to do just that. Fortunately, you slip and fall when you're just five or six feet off the ground. Falling that quickly means you still have strength left to loudly groan and rub your sore backside.

Nowhere in the world is there a god of sobriety and calculation, so you invent him yourself. His name is Pi, and his prayer is the multiplication table. Now you can sit back and await his mathematical blessing.

How many times have you told yourself not to sleep without a handkerchief covering your mouth? Well, one awful jaunt by a grass bug through your nose and out your mouth will make sure you never again forget to cover your head on the islands!

You notice barely legible letters in the tree bark. Running your finger over them, you try to figure out what they say and finally read: "Pierston was here." It looks like whoever that was carved his message back before the Cataclysm. What could have happened to him? And...what will you leave on Acribo when you're gone?

It must be nice being a tree. As long as there's a sun overhead and the occasional rain, you grow, blossom, and bear fruit. There's nothing to worry about besides shaking some pollen into the wind, dropping fruit on the ground, and stretching skyward. All you have to be afraid of is typhoons...well, and people with axes...
Having your own tree is much better than having, for example, a pet. Pets die sooner or later, while trees just keep growing and growing. Plus, you don't have to walk trees.

You climb higher and find a hollow in the tree. In fact, it looks like there's a mound of nuts inside. Could some nimble forest animal have prepared a treat for you? You reach in and realize that all it actually left for you was the shells...

The worst part of all this is the drops of resin on the bark and young buds. Your work-hardened hands aren't afraid of splinters or blisters, but sticky spots that attract all kinds of dirt drive you crazy.

You carefully touch the bark and realize that if you had to stand there all year round holding onto the ground with your roots, weathering storms, and fighting off lumberjacks and gatherers with your branches, you wouldn't just cover yourself in bark; you'd poison your bark, leaves, branches, and even fruit.

If you could pull whole layers of bark off the tree and it could grow new bark to replace what you stripped away, you could cover quite a large house with bark. Much better than the damp corner you have now.

As you try to clean the moss off a piece of bark, a hard brown edge slips right under your fingernail. When your scream finally echoes back to you, you're scared some kind of animal will come by looking to mate with you...

You find yet another inscription near the roots. Rows of numbers run off raggedly around the foot of the wooden giant. You try to read them but finally give up, the reason why they're illegible finally occurring to you: the inscription was made while lying down and stone-cold drunk. It looks like that's the only way to read it too...

Unfortunately, progress sometimes leads to the useful experience of our ancestors being lost. Just think of everything they used to make out of bark: medicine, tanning products, ink, roofs, shoes, baskets, and even paper. And there you are looking at it, and all you know how to do is eat it.

You cast a carpenter's appraising eye at the tree and can immediately tell how many boards you'll get from it, what the quality of the wood is, and what you can use that wood for. Yep...that's what's called experience. And to think that you'd never once touched a saw before the crash!

You've heard that islanders are much more likely to be killed by heavy nuts falling from palm trees than by poisonous snakes or sharks. Of course, that's no palm in front of you, but you can never be too careful. It's time to figure out what you can use for a helmet...
The tree creaks, sending dust and little chips flying out from under the bark. And, of course, the whole mess goes straight into your eyes! All you can do is rub them and blink violently.

It's hard to tell whose fault it is that dust accumulates under the bark, though it's either the tree itself or bark beetles. Whatever the case, you can't stop sneezing. Has anyone ever died of a never-ending fit of sneezes?
Dew might keep the dust down, so you figure you should get back to work early the next morning. Plus, bark beetle larvae are sleepy and easier to collect then...
Suddenly you realize you could carve plates out of the bark! You couldn't use them for soup, of course, but you could put, say, baked tubers in them without a problem.

You rip off a chunk of bark and focus on being a prudent land-owner. Everything has its place: big chunks go in the pile you'll use for the bungalow roof, little ones in the kindling pile, and middle-sized ones get set aside for you to make something out of later.

It's a shame the bark isn't thick enough. You can carve plates out of it, but cups would be much harder. And there's no point even thinking about a bucket. On the other hand, you can make lots of corks with it, so long as you have something to stick them in!

You look at the piece of bark and feel a bit of anger flare up at the fact that you have to yet again walk the path already tread by humanity. Nobody in the Empire makes roofs and dishes out of bark anymore! That was the past!

Memories suddenly cast you into a sad depression. When you were young, your father often took you to the market to see all the fun little things intricately carved from bark. How much time the local craftsmen must have spent on them... Here in Acribo there's no place for decorations; you just focus on getting the job done as quickly as possible.

On early spring day when you were little, you'd cut off a piece of bark, jab a stick into it, make a sail out of a dry leaf, and launch your ship in a cold puddle. Sadly, these days you have other things to do and worry about...

You haven't seen any larches in Acribo. That's a shame, since their wood is perfect for making furniture and different kinds of containers. It doesn't crack or split when you're working on it... You'll just have to make do with what you have...

Drying out the wood is the most important part. Otherwise you'd drag it off and create something, only to have cracks appear when it dries and ruin the whole thing. Sure, you haven't actually cut any wood yet, but there's still time for that!

You figure you could make a whole dinner set out of bark, though it might absorb smells. It sure would be strange to have a bowl of dried fish smelling like onion soup. Wash it or don't, the smell sticks. Maybe you could use some kind of oil finish?
You trip over a knotted root only to have it occur to you that you could carefully cut it into a nice pipe for smoking! An excellent find! If only your toe didn't hurt so much...

Lost in thought, you automatically stick a chunk of resin in your mouth. You spit it out quickly, gritting your teeth from the pain in your lower lip. Damn! Yet again you forgot to make sure there weren't any of the nasty biting insects people have told you often get stuck in resin.

You see an awful-looking toad in the grass only to have it suddenly remind you of that old fairy tale about the prince who kissed a frog that turned into a beautiful princess. Yep, princes always get lucky... The toad in front of you would probably turn into some kind of fat fish seller. No, thank you, no kisses today!

Your efforts are finally yielding a result: you're soaked in sweat that's even dripping off your eyelashes. You're about to wipe them dry, but a quick glance at your sleeve tells you they're better off drying on their own.

Your palms are covered in such thick callouses that the only sound clapping would make is a dull thud. You could get a nice ring if you knocked on your head, however. Better get to work and stop thinking about nonsense like that.

The tree's roots go so deep that it has to know if it's worth sinking a water pump here or not. Sadly, you don't speak tree... Some people, though, have said that after half a cup of celebrium sap they can talk with clouds, not to mention trees...

You suddenly notice the head of a nail sunk into the bark. Judging by the rust, it's been there for quite a while. But who could have hammered it in? And why? What were they making? Questions, questions without answers...

Exhaustion claims another victim. You drifted off while still standing upright and dreamed that the ground opened up under your feet, dropping you down to the bottom of the sea. When you got there, you saw that the tree's roots had transformed into the tentacles of a giant kraken. Your scream woke you up...
