No, probably better to avoid sleeping away from home on these islands...

You feel the trunk of the tree and think to yourself that it might not be the worst idea to plant some kind of sapling near your house. Still, you shouldn't let it grow into a giant like this one. Trees are always felled the same way, and all it would take is an especially strong hurricane...

You take your normal glance around the nearby trees, trying to figure out the best angle to chop them down from. That crooked one will definitely fall toward the leafy cover overhead, but what about the others?
There's one plus: a monster like that will crush you so fast you won't have time to feel upset about it. You'll crack open like a coconut beaten by a hammer.
You decided which side you wanted to start cutting into the tree from. The most important thing is to take your time so it falls where you need it to fall.
Yet again you find yourself wishing you had an assistant. The extra hands would be nice, and you wouldn't mind the advice either... And if it were a girl, you could even go without the advice...
Is it worth cutting off the branches on the side you want the tree to fall toward? It would lay flatter, but that's a lot of time to spend...
Really, it's much safer to take your time and cut trees down little by little, starting at the top. But that would take all day.

You try to remember the last time it rained... Maybe yesterday? It might be worth waiting until the evening to start work. Trees are heavier after it rains, meaning they're harder to cut down and the bark is more slippery.
You rest your palm on the rough bark and estimate how many boards you'll get from the tree. What a specimen! Not many left like this.

That's it. You did the near-impossible. It's odd, but a feeling of regret creeps over you as you look at the enormous stump. How would people live if they all left a stump like that in the ground when they died?

Uprooting stumps is much harder than cutting down trees. Maybe you should just wait for a typhoon to do the job for you? They say typhoons on the islands are so strong they rip up trees and roots all at once...
Well, the hole around the stump is ready. You sit down on the remains of the wooden giant and look at the roots you're going to have to just cut through. You aren't digging a well, after all!
The smell of fresh wood goes to your head. The same thing probably happens to hunters when they smell fresh blood...
You count the rings in the defeated giant and realize you're a measly barbarian who destroyed something many times greater and older than yourself.
Even in death the tree continues to hold tight to the earth. Maybe it's planning on soaking up rain and giving life to a new sprout?
Exhaustion grips your body, and a tempting thought creeps into your head: maybe you can try to burn the wooden octopus in front of you?
Working the ground is hard, and you either end up with a hernia or a broken back. The good news is that dying of starvation saves you from both of those fates.
The tree really was enormous! If you had more time, you could make an impressive boat out of its trunk! Although, to be fair, boats are a thing of the past; airships now rule from the skies...

The stump just shakes without giving in, and you're getting angry. Rivulets of sweat are pouring off you and your hands are shaking. A little more of this and you'll just chop the stump up into woodchips where it stands.
Chips fly as you saw away at the timber as if doing battle with some ancient monster. Keep going, victory is close!

The monotony begins to wear on you. People were created for something more, no? You were obviously not born to work in a sawmill... You really should have studied at the musical school your mom wanted you to go to!

The enormous log stretches out on the ground like some kind of beached whale. Fortunately, there's no danger of it rotting like a whale would, and you don't have to keep the steam jackals away from it. But you do need to do something with it. Where should you start?
Perfect, cutting your hand open on some rough bark is just what you needed. It's like the defeated giant is reaching back from the grave to avenge himself.

The saw keeps getting stuck in the damp wood, underlining yet again how much you need a partner. Sure, you could jump back and forth to either side of the log and do it that way, but you probably wouldn't last long.

It might be a good idea to make yourself some kind of gloves... Yet another splinter the size of a wood chip is sticking out of your palm. Then again, if this keeps up, the calluses and scars covering your hands will do the job quite nicely. Maybe you'll even be able to cut wood with your bare hands.
All you have for your long hours of hard work is a shallow notch. It's like the wood is laughing at you. But that's okay, he who laughs last laughs longest!
That last bit of extra effort damaged the saw. You kick the tree in frustration, conceding a temporary defeat. It gets a break while you try to fix the tool...

Now you have time to think about whether you prefer your sawdust wet or dry. Dry sawdust always gets in your hair and eyes, while your saw gets stuck in wet sawdust. On the other hand, it doesn't matter, since you have to just keep sawing either way.

It's always better when you can find a way to enjoy what you're doing. Even if that's working with your saw. You can admire the way the sun glints off the steel blade, for instance. You can listen to the even squealing made by its teeth. You can breathe in the scent of freshly cut wood. But, well, if you don't find any of that enjoyable, you'll just have to saw away without enjoying it.
The gnarled wood is so hard to saw through that you start to think about just leaving it for the bark beetles.
The screaming pain in your palm lets you know that you have another blister. You really need to spend a bit more time polishing and finishing that handle...

You think back to stories about trees that gave enough wood to build a large house. Realizing how much time and energy it would take to do all that by hand, you figure you'd be better off just finding a hollow tree and living in it.

You know, there's something unfair about all this. A seed grows into a sprout, which reaches toward the sky, puts out roots, and day by day grows higher and stronger until it turns into an enormous tree. And all it needs for that process is sun, soil, air, and water. You have all the same ingredients, but for you they aren't nearly enough.

Your father always said to take big jobs little by little. As usual, he was right. Anything can seem like too much at the beginning, though there comes a time when you realize the whole thing is already done.

Your father liked saying that if you wanted to eat, you had to work. You occasionally went all evening without dinner until your mom felt bad and brought you a bowl of steaming soup without your dad knowing. You didn't believe him until you joined the army...
A yellowish drop of resin looks like a bit of honey. It draws your eyes and you pull it off the bark it's stuck to and into your mouth. The smell and taste are better than coffee!
Once when you were little you planted a tree, never thinking that you'd one day be doing that semi-professionally. You would have done a better job listening to your dad if you had...
You plant the seedling and loosen the soil before watering it. Everything you do needs care and attention to detail, as you learned in your good, old army days.

You have to pluck off all the dead branches and smear clay over broken bark. Little trees are like little children, if a bit easier to take care of. Loosen the soil, water them, and that's just about it!
It'd be a good idea to add some manure to the soil. Nobody likes growing in poor earth, and the little plant could use some food.
Nothing can be left to chance. You have to find softer soil that's as high as possible. Otherwise it'll rain, overwhelm the roots, and drown your seedlings. Even water is only good in moderation.

You can't miss anything. The root collar needs to be a bit higher than ground level. Later the soil will settle, pulling everything to where it needs to go. Oh, and you shouldn't forget to plant your seedling with the spreading side facing the sun, just like how it used to grow.
Gently patting down the soil next to the sapling isn't the last thing you have to do, but what's most important is to go easy. It can't be too loose, but it shouldn't be rock-hard either.

If you weren't so civilized, you'd definitely kill a sacrifice and pour the fresh blood over the roots of the tree. As it is, you settle for spitting over your left shoulder and knocking on the bark. Who knows? Maybe that will help!
You should probably strip the old leaves from your sapling. They'll die as it is, and this way they won't suck strength and sap the rest of the tree needs.
You could kick yourself! How many times are you going to get a splinter stuck under a fingernail? It feels like there's a whole tree in there!
Now all that's left is to hope for the best. The sapling looks strong and healthy, but who knows... You did everything you could, but what if it went too long without soil?
A lateral root broke off when you were planting the sapling. You pick it up and see a vibrant, juicy, white fracture. Excellent: the tiny tree is breathing and growing. You picked a good one.
You stroke the bark and wonder about the feeling of calm you get when you're around the tree. Could it be a coincidence that ancient healers built strong relationships with trees and other plants?

In Acribo you're starting to think that all things are like a tree as it begins from a tiny seed, grows into a fragile sapling, and gradually reaches toward the light. Who knows where those thoughts come from...everyone you know would just laugh at them. Still, they keep coming...
You think to yourself that you should plant another tree next to this one if it takes root. If it doesn't, you should plant two more just to make sure.
You wander around the sapling and suddenly see something glinting in the dirt. The ancient past is once again reaching out to you. What will Acribo give you this time?

They plant trees in the steppes to shelter fields from the wind, shade smaller plants from the sun, and protect the soil from dust storms. Here on the Acribos you need just two things from trees: shade and wood.

As you try to pull up the plants around your sapling, you clumsily yank on a supple leaf that slices deep into your finger. Creatures all defend themselves as best they can, even plants. But they can't all curse and stomp on their opponent in frustration!
A new find! What you thought was just another rock and even wanted to kick off into the distance turned out to actually be pretty valuable.

You trip and feel something squirm under your leg. Then that something tries to sink its teeth into your boot. You fastidiously trample the snake underfoot, thankful that even a steam jackal couldn't bite through your sporeboar-skin boots.

A gentle caramel aroma wafts out over the meadow, apparently from those pale pink flowers. It might be a good idea to pluck a sackful or two so you can make them into an invigorating brew. But first you'll have to make sure they aren't poisonous!

You see delicate white blossoms and walk right past them. They can just keep on growing... Bitter experience has taught you not to even touch them unless you want painful blisters to immediately pop up on your skin.

Sometimes you freeze and close your eyes. It seems like that makes it easier to revel in all the fabulous flavors wafting through the air: land, grass, flowers, moisture... The smells all join in a delectable bouquet.

You look at the fern's leaves and are pretty sure you remember that their blossoms show where treasure is buried. An uplifting thought... The one problem is that you know perfectly well that ferns don't blossom.

You notice a mushroom hiding in the grass and find that it's full of worms. Ah, the irony of fate! You somehow managed to come across a mushroom on the islands only to find that you were late to the party...

You suddenly stumble across some bushes wielding enormous greenish thorns in between their leaves. Be careful! You could very well scratch a finger and suck on the wound only to find that the thorns are poisonous...

Names slip off into the backwaters of memory, though tastes stay on your tongue forever. You must have picked those reddish berries at some point when you were little. Sure, they were sweeter then and more bitter now, but back then everything seemed sweeter.
You found an unusual plant whose buds resemble a small bonfire. Beautiful... Though the rotten smell coming from them tells you that you're better off not touching them.

Where the area is a little damper, you see a strange plant with glossy petals and putrid flowers covered in flies. It looks like the plant attracts flies from all over the place to catch and eat. What a good metaphor for the islands.

Picking up a heavy branch, you hack your way through a thicket of overgrown grass. Fat buds squelch, stalks break like dried snakes, and bees angrily buzz around... Ah, if only everything was this easy.

A lovely aroma reaches you from the other side of the meadow. Ah-ha: some little purple flowers are blossoming. You mercilessly stomp them to death. If the sporeboars eat them, their meat will be ruined completely. You've seen molds that smell fresher...

You suddenly come across a wild cabbage bush in the middle of the burdocks. Crouching down on your knees, you note that the delicate leaves are covered in caterpillars... Why do they always have to eat what you like instead of all the other trash?

You suddenly remember a boatswain you met once on an airship... As he said, reasonably and with feeling, "Be careful with the plants on the islands! They may not smell like much, but you'll just keep sniffing away until you can't sniff anymore. Then you'll realize your head is completely empty—just shout and listen to the echoes chasing each other. Terrifying!"
Burning grass burns, bitter grass is bitter, and soapy grass lathers. But this one makes itchy blisters pop up all over your hands! So would it be right to call it "blistery"?

The thousands of flowers around you have filled the air with some kind of unbelievable aroma that has your head spinning a bit... You pluck one of them and, as if in a dream, stick it in your mouth...
Plants don't live very long. Today they're green and full of sap, and tomorrow they're dry and brittle. Just look at the blade of grass you plucked and ground into dust between your fingers.

The grass is full of insects. And the ones that don't sting just stink. Obviously, that's how they fend off would-be predators. You may accidentally squish one once, but you certainly won't make that same mistake twice.

The most dangerous insects in Acribo are forest hornets. They're like wasps, just much bigger. It's wise to keep your distance, as swatting one of them out of force of habit leaves your arm paralyzed for a week in the best-case scenario.
You do your best to carefully pull plants up by the roots rather than just tearing off the leaves. While you generally come away with a clump of dirt, every once in a while you find edible tubers.

You try to snap open a burr in one practiced motion, but it turns out to be as hard as a rock. Again you forgot how the plants on these islands can be completely different from the ones you knew back home!
If there's one thing that's never let you down, it's these blades of grass. But you have to tramp your way through more than one field before you've eaten enough to feel full...

Crimson berries hide under the wide leaves. You can even lie on your back in the grass and eat them without using your hands... It's in moments like these when life in Acribo seems like nothing but fun, fun, fun all year round...

You're lying on the grass when you suddenly hear something rustling in the grass. A reddish, brownish bug with an enormous horn came trundling out into the meadow and doesn't appear anxious to share it with you. It jabs you in the knee threateningly, regardless of the fact that it's smaller than your hand. You realize that bravery like that deserves respect and politely head off to the side.
You bend over, peek under the bush, and freeze. Did you really get that lucky? What a rare ingredient!

The berries you came across are so sweet you can't stop until you've polished off the last one. Only then are you startled to hear the gurgling coming from your stomach. You should have thought to be more careful sooner!

In the moments when it seems like you just don't have the strength to deal with everything fate sends your way, it's best to close your eyes, breathe in the freshness of nature, and listen to the chirping of birds and the rustling of the wind. Then just open your eyes and start all over!

Sometimes it seems like there should be something among all these herbs, roots, and fruits you can use as the main ingredient for an immortality elixir. Sadly, you aren't able to find it. Your only consolation is that you don't know what the other ingredients are either...
It would be nice to find a philosopher's stone you could use to turn rocks into gold. Like all problems, it's best to take it little by little. You can start by finding the rocks...

When you were little, you were constantly being yelled at for the grass stains on your pants. Now all your clothes are covered in pollen and grass stains. Good thing there's nobody around to yell at you...
A long time ago your mom thought you'd be a musician. Sadly, there's nothing left of her dream, as your callused fingers are only good for plugging holes in barrels.

Back when you were little, you loved sneaking plants you picked on the street into your mom's soup. That's probably when you found your passion for new and uncharted discoveries. If you hadn't been kicked out of the kitchen, maybe you would have found the recipe for the elixir of eternal youth...

Most important is that the material turns out the way you want it to. For example, these stalks are too dry to bend, which means you should have started working on them earlier. Maybe if you soaked them for a while though...
It would be a good idea to find a long vine. They're just as strong as a good rope, though, unfortunately, that's only true as long as they're more or less fresh.
You find exactly what you need. These stalks are nice and flexible, and good materials are half the battle!

Your uncle always said that even bad tools can work miracles in capable hands. At least, he said that until one day his hammer actually fell apart in his hand. He was holding it above his head at the time, and he suffered from headaches for quite a while afterward.

You mechanically pull a berry off a bush and toss it into your mouth. It turns out to be as bitter as a cinchona. Yup, on these islands you need to stop trusting the instincts you've had since you were a kid and start thinking before you act...

You think back to the different kinds of knots you know, trying to figure out which would be best for right now. Reef? Fishing? Double loop? In the end, you go with a sheet bend, deciding that it's strong and still easy to untie.

You see exactly the kind of switch you need. The sapling is supple, but you're stubborn, bending it over and trying to twist it up out of the earth. That turns out to be a bad idea: the stalk suddenly slips out of your hands and smacks you right between the legs...
You can make strong rope out of hair, tendons, or different kinds of plants. The strongest, however, is probably the kind you make out of hemp.
As you search for materials, you walk right into a spider web. If only you could have that spider make your rope for you. You'd even agree to catch flies for it in exchange.
You repeat to yourself over and over again how important it is to watch where you're walking. You've come across your most interesting finds that way, after all. And now you found something unusual.
Somehow you didn't notice that snag hidden in the grass. Your foot catches on it and sends you sprawling, and you barely avoid turning your nose into a pancake.

When you were young, you had lots of dreams, including one that had you pursuing a career as a sailor. Bringing spices and amazing fruits back from exotic countries in a sailboat seemed the height of happiness. Now, having tasted travel in airships, all you can do is smile when you think of your childhood naivete...

Your hands are covered in armor-like calluses, though the rope slips along your palms, finds weak spots, and cuts through the chinks in the armor. Blood drips down onto the ground. It occurs to you that you've spilled enough blood for the local flora to slowly turn into vampires...
You're getting good at weaving ropes: you collect and dry plants, soaking, kneading, shaking, rubbing, and scratching them before starting to weave them together.

Some nice, tall hemp would be great for the rope. You can tear off the leaves and cut the stalk lengthwise to get a good, strong starting point. Cutting the stalk can be tricky though, as you can't go too deep or too shallow.
Even bark can work as a rope, so long as you have long, narrow strips.
You know that you have to grind dried strands, thoroughly work them over, and then twist them tightly. The better you do all that, the stronger the rope will be.
Hemp is another good plant for making rope. The problem is that you have to find female bushes; male bushes are better used for making cloth.
You cast your eyes around looking for a juicy bush. They put down roots faster after being transplanted.

Your mom told you that people didn't use to ever pull up anything in the forest without asking the spirits for permission. Stupid superstitions! Forests are nature's storerooms, and you are their master!
You crawl into the windbreak and barely have time to duck and shield your eyes with your hand. It's like the branches are aiming for your face!
What luck! You see something right near your feet that has no business being in a forest. Especially here on the islands. Who could have dropped it?
You don't particularly enjoy gardening, given all the hassle it involves, though homemade food always reminds you of how well your mom cooks and how good her apple and pear pastries were.

You take a couple seconds to think about whether it's worth praying to the ancient goddess of fertility for a better harvest. Then you smile and realize that you're better off spending that time fertilizing the soil.
Scouring the ground is so tedious. You massage your neck, realizing how tense it's gotten.

You see a bug lying helplessly on its back and waving its legs around. Picking up a branch, you reach it out toward the little guy. The bug grabs it, you quickly yank it up into the air, and you flick the branch, sending the bug off like a miniature airship.
You hear a sharp crack and freeze. What was that? A trap? An enemy? A sporeboar? A landslide? You look around cautiously. Nothing. That's when you realize the crack came from a branch you stepped on.

Finally, a plant you can use. You grab the stem, pull, and then yank on it. The roots hold firm in the ground and you end up losing some skin from your palms. Maybe pulling up a bush with your bare hands wasn't the best idea.

You look closer at what appears to be a horsetail, a plant found only rarely on the island. Your mom's words come back to you: "Where gold fell like hail, there grows a horsetail." Silly, but still worth checking the area for gold, no?
You try to remember if you're supposed to make a cough elixir from purple flowers. The ones the color of ripe pumpkins are excellent for wrapping wounds, right?

Your mom always told you to respect the earth, seeing as how everything feeds off it and takes its strength from it. Your father added that you can cut down and pull up plants for the same reason: it lightens the load for the earth.

Bugs love eating all things green and fresh. But smart farmers remember to sow and fertilize at the right times, not to mention setting up special alchemical traps at the corners of their plots to catch pests.
What wouldn't you do to make sure your plants grow strong and healthy? One example is getting rid of the moles in your land. Those rascals love digging everything up and gnawing on the roots!

Before you start fussing around the garden, it's important to find an agriculturalist or, if nothing else, an alchemist. They'll be able to explain the order in which you should plant everything. Another alternative is to become an agriculturalist yourself, of course...
What an idiot! You thought the nettle wouldn't sting so painfully now that it's yellowed...
You've never seen leaves and berries like those. It would be a good idea to show them to an alchemist or a naturalist, so you break off a branch laden with a cluster of the large, crimson berries.
You move the foliage aside and find a few ripe berries. They're so juicy! You bite into them and feel your thirst being quenched.
A sharp pain pierces your leg. What was that?! It turns out you stepped on the tail of a large lizard that quickly took vengeance on you.
How many times have you been struck by the wisdom and skill of nature? It made these perfect spinners: through the branches you see the cocoons of caterpillars hanging on thin but rugged threads.

Fine silk clothes used to only be available for noblemen, though now anyone who's willing to work hard enough can have them. Just go find some cocoons and unravel them yourself. At least, that's what's on your mind as you search for another cocoon.

Unraveling silkworm cocoons isn't the easiest thing in the world to do. But you aren't in a hurry. First you need to find as many as you can, and then you'll heat up a strong solution, boil them, soften them, and then begin to unravel the thin, almost invisible strands.

You look closer at the branches and wonder to yourself who could have thought to use silk threads. Why did they think of that? You heard somewhere that some nomads from the south sold the secret to the first emperor for a few chests of gold, though it could just as easily have been the first academics...

As you stand by the tree with the cocoons, you realize that you've never seen what comes out of the silk prisons. A wonderful day wanderer with stunningly beautiful wings or a plain shadow using its gray shades to hide in the night?
Something flew by not far away. Could it be a silk moth? You watch its flight intently in the hopes of seeing where cocoons are hanging.
Finding a moth is already a good start. Over the course of a summer, several generations of silkworms are born, so one can tree might house moths, caterpillars, and cocoons all at once.
You see trees that looked like they were stripped bare in a fire. That's the work of caterpillars. The little gluttons don't move on until there isn't a single living leaf left on the tree.
Cocoons are like little works of art. You're so impressed by the hard-working insects who take all of four days to make their silk houses.
Silkworms are something like people: the males make their cocoons with thick, heavy walls, while the females prefer more delicate homes.
The cocoons, snow-white, weightless, fragile, lie on your palm. You couldn't find anything like them anywhere in the world except on these islands.

You're exhausted, but you still haven't been able to find any good cocoons. You did come across a clump of ripe berries, so at least there's that. Stuffing them happily into your mouth, you swallow, barely giving yourself enough time to taste them.

You happily throw yourself at the tree. A cocoon! You grab it and scowl in disappointment: it's just another of the thousands of regular caterpillar cocoons in the forest. Slapping it against the trunk of the tree in frustration, you smush the cocoon into a sticky slime.
As you move aside the branches, you bend one back until it slips and whips you across the face. You grab your cheek with a cry. Blood!

If silkworms can make threads out of the leaves of silk trees, a concoction of silk berry juice must be able to work miracles. It probably heals all wounds, not to mention all diseases... You should give that a try!

You're tired and annoyed. Collecting cocoons didn't turn out to be as simple as you thought it would be, and you're going to need an entire mountain of them to get the amount of cloth you're looking for. Maybe it's time to give up and find something else to do?

Of all the different ways to tell what kind of year you're going to have, you only remembered one: you're supposed to find a mulberry tree and see if it has any fresh sprouts. If it does, the year will be warm. Interestingly, Acribo doesn't have mulberry trees, though it's always warm here. Every single year...
You take extra care handling this chrysalis. But the butterfly burns the cocoon with its saliva and pops out, rendering it completely useless.

All kinds of thoughts pop into your head when it's this hot. For example, you were just wondering if everyone has their own predetermined thread of fate. Is there a way to elongate them? Can you try to stretch yours out and last longer than you're supposed to?

The open wound is terrifying, but you quickly gather your wits. You have to stop the bleeding and cauterize or bandage the wound. Leaving it like that is just inviting infections to work their way through your body.
You have to wash the wound. But you don't have anything you can use for that... Wait, what about urine...? Sure, it's unpleasant, but if it helps...
How do you get rid of the pain? Think! Remember! City doctors would give you morphine or opium, but here? Belladonna? You're pretty sure you saw some nearby.
You can cauterize puncture wounds by putting wax on them and applying hot metal. Lacerations need to have hanging fragments of flesh removed and then be cleaned with boiling wine.
Sometimes you could really use a first-aid kit with everything you need in situations like these: bandages, syringes, scalpels, a curved needle to sew up wounds, sutures...

If you could only remember what Dr. Helmund taught you! He was a masterful, unflappable man. He'd operate away, not even flinching when bullets flew overhead, and he kept a pipe puffing away in his mouth the whole time.

Everything is mixed up in your head: the wounded man is barely breathing, and you're terrified you'll finish him off. Should you start by cauterizing the wound? Or tie a splint to the broken extremity? Should you wake him up or let him lie there unconscious for the time being?

First aid is just one more thing you have to do. If a person loses their senses, you wake them up with an unexpected smell: break a swamp reed under their nose or let them sniff a smoldering clump of hair. If they have a broken bone, brace the limb with two sticks and tie them together with a rope. If they're gushing blood, wrap a rag around the wound and then work around the edges to switch in a clean cloth.

They say that when someone's head is chopped off, it still understands what's going on and even blinks as it rolls around. Once in battle you personally saw someone sliced nearly in half charge forward, though each leg was pulling its half of the body in a different direction...

Nothing could stand in the way of the carnage wreaked by steam tanks and walking flamethrower machines. The whole field is strewn with shattered bodies, and they all have white bones jutting out of them like the joints of burnt toys. Even the vultures are kept away by the stink of metal and charred flesh.
Don't even think about dying! You think I've been hunched over you this long for nothing? You'll heal up like a steam jackal!

The boatswain liked telling war stories. "In that battle we had to go up against tin golems. They're a merciless breed and they chewed through us like a mower through grass, leaving the rangers behind them to shoot whoever was left with their muskets."

Dr. Helmund always gave you a choice: take a sip of poppy dew that might make you go crazy or suffer with a belt between your teeth. At least he cleaned wounds out quickly and easily, almost as lightly as if he was doing it with a feather, and he didn't lose a single soul on his table.
We had one guy with half his face taken clean off by a gunshot. They stuck a leather half-mask to his face later and he looked better than when he started. A huge hit with the ladies.
Cheap wine or liquor will only make things worse right now. Your blood will boil and you'll go a bit crazy. But that's your business.

Be honest, how scared are you? Why are you shaking like that? We'll give you something fiery to drink and that'll get you feeling nice and warm inside. That's death grabbing you by the scruff of the neck. Get out, damn it!

You've seen so much on these godforsaken islands! A sporeboar once ripped open someone's stomach to the point where their intestines spilled out onto the ground. Someone else had their head shot off only to have their body keep walking forward until it realized... Nothing can get to you anymore.

The most important thing is to stay on your feet when you catch a shot like that. Everyone who survives gets there! Everyone who falls is left to lie there. Some, of course, crawl, but we aren't reptiles, after all!
You stretch your legs and think to yourself how nice it would be next to a fire or maybe a melting furnace... Then you'd be able to get warm and dry your clothes...
An enormous yawn engulfs your face as you sit down, and you happily scratch away at all your different itches. Sure, it's not how gentlemen behave, but there aren't any gentlemen in Acribo.
You stretch so hard your joints crackle, and give a wide yawn. The weary muscles are filling with languor.

You stretch your legs and wiggle your toes, thinking how nice it would be to make or trade for some comfortable shoes. They may not be Cardin's finest, but they'd certainly be better than rough boots made from sporeboar skin...
Wouldn't it be great to have a full meal? Mom's hare soup...ah, food of the gods! Your eyes close as you immerse yourself in vivid memories...
It's so nice to just sit here and relax, you think. You didn't have any time to sit when you were serving in Wildhost...

All it takes for all kinds of weird thoughts to come into your head is for you to sit down... Will the Emperor appreciate the feats of your expedition? Is it true that ancient powers hold sway over the islands? Will you ever go home?
You don't forget to touch the ground before sitting down on it. Wet earth never did anyone any good. The only thing worse to sit on is cold stones.
You let your eyes close for a brief moment, reminding yourself not to fall asleep, but it's as if dreams glue your eyelids shut and your nose begins to droop.
As you rub your arms and shoulders, you think to yourself about finding some warmer clothing.
You think how nice it is sometimes to sit with friends around the fire telling tall tales and remembering your glorious past.

On the ground you see ants scurrying around. How does such a small insect find the strength to lift blades of grass ten times heavier than itself when people need steam technology to do the same? You carefully lift up on the blade in a gentle attempt to share the load, but the ant lets go and runs off. It prefers to do all the work itself.

Your hands continue to work even when your thoughts take you far away. At the moment you're drawing mindless patterns in the ground in front of you using a sharp twig. Maybe there's somebody hidden inside you trying to communicate?

You look at your hands and see wiry veins covering the backs of your hands like rivers of blue. Hard work spares no one — your skin gets rough, your arms get veined, and you get black grime underneath your fingernails.
Your father used to say: "Find time for work, but be sure to leave an hour for leisure." The wise old man knew life well.
Your heart seems to be skipping beats in your chest. You really have to take a break...

You love just sitting there and letting your daydreams wash over you. You're already back home, with all the benefits of civilization at your fingertips. Sitting in your favorite pub, you imperiously wave a hand to the waiter, having forgotten that there's nobody actually there to hurry over...

Something's digging into your hip. Puzzled, you stick your hand in your pocket and pull out a whimsical little stone with lovely markings along one side. How could it have ended up in your pocket...? And how many million years did it take the sea to turn it into a near-perfect oval? If you bored a hole in the middle, it would be perfect for wearing around your neck. Only because it looks good, of course; no superstition here!
You cover your eyes with your hands, tired of staring into the reflections glinting off the surface of the water... Oh, come on! Your eyes are closed, but you still see red and white flashes...
You examine the ground in order to check for fresh tracks — perhaps some light paws have left their prints somewhere.
It occurs to you that it would be easier to set a trap for small prey than to go hunting. A trap can save a lot of effort!
You set your trap and think that catching an animal requires a lot of patience. The beast has to get used to the place, smell everything, and eventually decide everything is safe…

You mark the place where you set the trap and think you should check it more often. Sometimes you fail to check the trap in due time, and the prey has already escaped! Either that, or it got eaten by a larger beast.
You think of how important it is to find a good place for your trap. A narrow path with overhanging branches is perfect — the beast will tear through the shrubs and will definitely get into the trap.
Startling an animal is another good method. It will run into any trap in its terror, no matter how roughly you may make it.

From the hunting legends an old captain's mate told you, you know you can't disturb the environment around you, for instance, by breaking branches or brushing away leaves. That puts animals on the alert, leaving them prone to running off before you can ever fire a shot.
You examine the trap you've just set and cover it with leaves and dirt.
It occurs to you that you might want to use some smoke from a fire to make sure no trace of human smell remains anywhere.
You check whether the trap you've set is sturdy enough. Any minute defect can be used by the animal to its advantage.
If you set the trap a bit higher, as the boatswain on the airship taught you, no forest predator will be able to reach the prey.
A nice, fat turkey would be perfect. You could roast it over the fire...ah, it would be delicious!
As you set the trap, you have a good feeling that this time you're going to get lucky. It'll be a great catch!
You check to make sure you didn't leave too little bait. To be fair, steam jackals can smell it from a mile away, so you decide not to risk using any more. No point attracting those scavengers...
The pole that you intended to use for the bait unbends suddenly and slaps you right in the face. You reach for the sore cheek trying not to show how painful it was.
There are quite a few delicious turkeys on the islands. Some of them are even so big, the trap might not hold them. You'd better test it to see if you need thicker bars.

You set your trap right on a path that has fresh animal tracks. You know that in the morning such tracks are usually moist — there can even be water inside them. But by the afternoon they crumble at the lightest touch.
What would you do if you were in a turkey's shoes? You think about that and try to crawl through the thicket. Okay, maybe that wasn't the brightest idea...

You test the pole's flexibility by bending and unbending it. Lianas are best — there is so much moisture in them that you could probably tie a knot in the branch. Celebrium branches would be even better, but they are poisoinous.
These tracks were obviously left by a sporeboar.
You bend down to take a closer look at the complex pattern of prints left by birds.
You try to leave your own footprint on the path out of sheer curiosity. But it turns out very vague and hardly visible at all — the ground here is dense and compact.
It looks like a steam jackal ran by here. But it's hard to read their tracks, since they're always going around in circles.

Hunting is a competition. The animal is trying to save its skin; you're trying to save your stomach. Well, to be fair, when it comes to some animals you have to worry about saving your skin too. You look around and try to figure out how to avoid becoming the prey. Do animals themselves think about these things too?

You slip on a rotten piece of wood and flail your arms around as though you were trying to get airborne. You grab branches with your fingers and scream with pain. You have managed to keep your balance, after all, but it seems like you have sprained your ankle.
A sharp pain makes you stop in your tracks and lift your left leg. Your foot has failed to avoid a sharp stone, which injures the sole badly. How are you supposed to keep walking now?
You remember a story from one of the past expeditions: One of the soldiers tried to track a partridge into the woods, but he never came back.
You start as you hear a strange sound. Was that an owl? Or an airship's steam engine? You forget the tracks and warily peer up into the sky.
You startled a parrot, and it has started to chatter loudly. You throw a ball of earth into the bird — if it carries on like this, it will scare all the animals away!
A twig snaps under your foot, breaking the silence. You kick the piece of wood in frustration — it has announced your presence to all the animals around.
As you scan the ground around you, you see a piece of scrap metal and pick it up, figuring that it will come in handy.
You were so engrossed in that new, exotic tree that you didn't notice yourself trampling all over the animal tracks.

You suddenly feel something moving under your collar. Whatever it is, it's crawling around and trying to bite you. A tick or some kind of poisonous bug is just what you need right now! You rub your back up against a prickly stalk as hard as you can. The smaller the parasite, the more dangerous it is!
You take an awkward step and twist your foot. You squat, rubbing your sprained ankle. Forget about Wildhost sidewalks!
You know so few of the plants here in the jungle. Some of their fruits could be completely edible... But who can you try them out on?
Your foot sinks underground, and you barely manage to avoid breaking it. You swear to yourself and continue on your way.

Your blood runs cold and you freeze when you see animal tracks on the path. You gingerly place your foot in one of the enormous prints left behind and nearly swoon in horror. Your foot isn't even half as big as it is! You look around and listen carefully. Who's hunting who?

Hunting is easy for anyone who's served in the imperial air fleet. Still, it isn't worth going too deep into the Acribian forests. Everyone knows the story about the soldier who tracked a turkey into the woods and never came back.
One thing is certain — you wouldn't want to come face to face with a pack of steam jackals.
You take a closer look at the ground... These tracks were definitely left by a sporeboar. But they are rather old.

You lean up against a tree to scratch your back only to look up and see enormous claw marks twice your height up on the tree. It seems your stomach is suddenly feeling a bit queasy. Oh, and your throat is dry.
You see that the leaves are trampled, but it's hard to tell where the beast went.
You're too busy looking around to notice the thick branch you walk straight into.

That looks like a dog's track in the soil. A steam jackal! You think back to the stories of how the Acribians made them for protection or sport, though you can't remember which. One thing is for sure: a meeting with one of them wouldn't end well.
You see tracks left by a spoarboar. But the beast must have been in a hurry. Who was following it?
Hunters need to know everything: how to tell different animals apart by the remains of their prey, by the way plants look after they've walked over them, and even by their excrement.
Running into a single steam jackal is no good as it is. But if you ever come across a pack of them, well, you're a goner!
The silence is broken by the sudden crack of a branch. Good work: yet again, you scared off all the animals in the area with your carelessness.
If you think about it, meeting a pack of steam jackals or a singular of sporeboars can only end one way...
Sometimes it seems like animals are smarter than people. You sneak along behind this one and realize that you're going in circles. Chills run down your spine.
The sporeboar smells strange, something between an animal and a plant. Ever since the Ancients cursed these islands, everything's been upside down.
You remember that sporeboars are more than just meat and prey; they're a great way to pick up some nice cuts, scrapes, and broken bones.
You're following the round, clawed tracks, but they suddenly disappear. You look up slowly, but there's nothing in the sky. Thank the gods. Who knows what that creature was...
Coming across some tooth marks in a tree that had fallen across the path, you measure the size of the mouth with your fingers. It looks like your whole head could fit inside.

Without forgetting to keep an eye on the ground, you soak in the harsh, powerful, and heavy atmosphere of the Acribian jungle. It reeks of danger. So many years have passed since the Cataclysm, but its effects are visible to this day.
You masterfully slice open your prey's large veins to drain out the blood. From there it's like clockwork, as this isn't your first time.
You straighten up wearily, inspect your handiwork, and think that the old captain's mate on your crashed airship would have been proud of your butchering skills.
Butchering sporeboars is just as easy as butchering regular boars. There's nothing to it.
Better not put off cutting up the meat. In the jungle, and especially at this temperature, it goes bad quickly.

You wipe the edge of your knife. All professions have their most important tool, and for hunters that's their knife. You can't lose it, break it, or forget to take care of it. There's no doing without one. That's precisely why they sew different sheaths, tie on handles, and secure them with thick cords. A good knife is sometimes worth your life.

Each subsequent animal you kill will be more neatly skinned than the last, but you need to do your best from the very beginning. Cut and stretch carefully. It's dirty work, but it has to be done. There's a use for everything.
Most important is to stay away from the guts. If you cut open the stomach, spleen, or especially the gallbladder, you'll be too nauseous to actually eat anything. The whole thing will be ruined.
There was a time when you didn't enjoy hunting... The worst part was lugging your kills all the way home. Now it takes you just a few minutes to cut up the carcass right there on the spot.
You do a pretty good job with the dirty work. The guts are intact, so the meat is still good. You're no master hunter, of course, but you're getting there.

Things don't always go according to plan, unfortunately. You cut yourself, but the fact that your blood is mixing with the blood of the animal you're butchering means you can't tell how deep the cut is.

Your attention is suddenly drawn to a bald patch on the animal's hide. The poor thing hadn't had it easy even before you got to it. The patch looks like a healed wound from an arrow or even from a spear. The work of the natives?
Blood is caking on your hands, but it'll easily wash off in the nearby stream. You think less about how you've joined the food chain as a predator and more about how to stay on top of it.

You could have done a better job skinning your prey. It looks like you're going to have to go over it one more time to remove the membrane on the inside. Some salt would help, as it would keep the hide from stiffening or rotting.

The life leaves the body of your kill along with the warmth and blood. The heart no longer beats, though blood suddenly spurts from an artery and splashes all over your face. A less-than-pleasant feeling...

It's important to know how to skin animals too. You don't want to damage it, especially since skinning large animals is different from skinning small ones. You can't just pull the hide off a large carcass...
Exhausted, you sit down on the ground and think about how people groups all prefer different kinds of meat. Hungry people, however, have no such preferences. They just eat whatever they can find.

It turns out that cutting up a carcass is tricky when you don't know how. But you're still young. If you learn the trick to it, you'll soon be able to butcher them in minutes. Most important is to have a sharp knife.

Some days nothing goes right. The job's more or less done, but you feel weighed down by exhaustion. The carcass is cut up, but you don't feel good about it. A seaside vacation would probably help...if you weren't by the sea already.

You slowly walk around your construction site. No, you aren't going to make any sacrifices to the gods or bury a gold coin in every corner, though... Acribo has its own laws... It might a good idea just to make sure.

You remember the old construction tricks: jabbing a needle into a raw egg and leaving it in a wall or putting a bottleneck in a pipe. If the owner doesn't pay the builder, the latter can just pull out the needle or readjust the bottleneck and the owner will either have an unbearable stink in the house or a howling sound any time there's even the slightest breeze. But you're building something for yourself, no?

You figure your house should face the sea. Not because you believe in a higher power, the Ancients, or some kind of superstition; you just think that the breeze coming in from the water will bring in fresh, cool sea air.

You can make houses out of anything. Some earth houses can stand for decades, just so long as they aren't somewhere it rains every other day. You don't want to find yourself standing in a puddle of mud after every downpour.

Construction always begins with the foundation, unless, of course, you're building on top of solid rock. There are lots of issues you have to keep in mind, though you can rule one of them out here in the Acribos: how the foundation will weather the winter.
People like to give names to their personal weapons. Steamers and airships all have a name. Even rich villas are named. Maybe you should name your little house?

You scratch your head as you think back to make sure you didn't forget anything. You picked a spot that doesn't get fogged in, and it can be defended from the air... The ground is dry and firm, and that's all you can ask for.

You caress the tree trunk and think how you would cut it down in the winter, lay it out on the frame, and wait for it to dry if you were back on the mainland. Here in Acribo there's no winter to speak of, so it's not worth the trouble.

Most important is to find good-quality wood. It can't have any rotten areas or knots, and it needs to be even... Warped wood is hard to make into walls in the first place, and even if you're successful, you have to live with warped walls...
It isn't enough to just have a high, dry place for your house. You also need to check the wind, have shade trees nearby, and be far enough away from standing water...

You're still racked by doubts. Maybe you should wait another year or so? That way you could see if that volcano definitely went out and if serious typhoons happen around here. Maybe you should be building a yacht instead of a house?
You, obviously, are anything but superstitious, but maybe it's worth dropping a coin underneath the corners of the house? Just in case? You can call it a good investment in the future...
Well, that's interesting: the wood seems warm and the stone cold, though sticking a thermometer up against them shows that they're the same temperature. Everything in the world is relative...

You wonder what kind of timber you should use for the top of the building and the roof trusses. Tastes differ, but your favorite wood comes from aspens. The trouble is, there are no aspens on these islands, so you have to make do with whatever there is.
You should probably go for soft wood. The trunks are straighter and drier, not to mention the fact that it's easier to work with...
Trust, but verify. You chop into the log and feel a chip that flies off. If it's raw, the beams in your house could shrink or, worse, warp. What would happen to your window frames then?
Maybe you should build a stone house? Sure, it's damper, but then you wouldn't have to be afraid of an ember leaping out of the fire! It would also be cooler in this heat.
Stone homes are much safer. They're damp, sure, but none of the different Acribian animals would be able to get in, and your enemies wouldn't be able to just burn you out!

The important thing is to avoid skimping on anything. You're building for yourself, after all. The walls should be thick, the foundation should be deep, the ceiling should be high. The windows should be narrow, on the other hand. It might even be better to trade them in for loopholes!

You figure that if you run out of wood or stone, you can use straw or dry reeds. Just mix them up with some clay and mold what you need. It wouldn't last that long in this climate, but sometimes you don't have a choice.
You would make a decent neighbor or even friend. Well, so long as nobody bothers you in the morning, in the evening, or when you're hungry. There's no accounting for what you'll do then.
When your stomach is empty, you can hear how food and drinks run down into it. When it's been hungry for a long time, there's nothing to hear since the walls of your stomach stick to each other.

Suddenly it occurs to you that you're starting to forget what your mom's food tastes like. You try to remember, but your mouth fills with stringy saliva and you give up on what turned out to be a dangerous idea. You could choke!

When people are full, they don't eat; they feast. They roast meat on coals and bake things in clay pots. They ferment vegetables and savor them. They pull out pickled produce and jam. Hungry people just eat.

When you're hungry, you have to be careful not to choke. There usually isn't anyone around to bang away at your back; instead, you have to throw yourself against a tree. Thankfully, that worked this time...
Coughing and sneezing with a full mouth is also dangerous. You hate to see hard-earned food spraying everywhere when you sneeze...

As you try to wipe your lips, you accidentally press a wasp against one of them only to have it sting you. Your lip swells up and eating becomes nearly impossible. Each bite takes an enormous amount of work that could only be described as torture.

Life on the islands has taught you to listen to what's happening in your stomach. Sometimes you eat something or drink unboiled water and realize that it's time to run off somewhere, pulling down your pants as you go.

The worst is when you bite your cheek or tongue. It takes forever for them to heal, and you have to be careful how you bite down for a while afterward... You're in too much of a hurry just once and you can't enjoy your food for a week.

What bothers you most is what will happen if your appendix swells up or your teeth start to hurt. Your appendix, obviously, is more dangerous. You definitely won't be able to operate on yourself, though you might be able to pull or knock a tooth out. You know, the best plan is just to stay healthy!
Hunger is the best seasoning to any food! That's for sure... You'd gobble up anything right now, with no salt or pepper.
You feel a sudden weakness in your body, and a sweat comes onto your brow. Falling ill is the last thing you need right now.
Sometimes unpleasant sounds in your stomach don't mean you ate something bad. They often just mean you haven't eaten anything at all.
Good thing your stomach doesn't have its own memory. Otherwise it would torture you for a week every time you ate something nasty.
You dally for a moment, wary of another stomach cramp. You never know, after all... Oh well, better not think about it: whatever jumps into your mouth is good for you!
Life is always better when you have some food in you, even if it's just a little. The heat is less oppressive, the sun doesn't beat down quite so mercilessly...
"That's better," you think finishing the last bit. You have a talent for stuffing your stomack, there's no arguing about that!

Basic Knowledge
The Acribos.
An archipelago full of secrets, anomalies and destructive storms.
You won't find it on the Imperial maps.
Many followed ancient legends in search of these mysterious islands.
But their expeditions, one after another, disappeared without a trace.
But then came technological progress, and with it - steam engines
With their help, Imperial pilgrims finally managed to reach the Acribos.
On the very first night, the Victorian camp was attacked by the Acribians,
the islands' indigenous people.
This was the beginning of a long and bloody war,
the result of which was the enslavement of the rebels.
The Acribos became the Empire's colony.
Scientists began exploring the conquered lands.
They discovered that the sap of local trees called Celebrium
is a unique source of energy.
It's heating value is hundreds of times greater than that of coal and wood.
Celebrium shipments to Victoria grew exponentially.
It's power had no limits.
Soon, scientists encountered yet another mystery:
they found traces of an advanced civilization.
The discovered scrolls described how to fuse mechanisms with living flesh
with the help of Celebrium.
Supposedly, this increased resilience of the human body
and made animals stronger and more docile.
Immediately after that,
the Emperor authorized the beginning of surgical experiments
on the colonial slaves.
The scrolls also mentioned the bloody cult of the Enlightened,
which the people of the Acribos had been practicing many centuries ago.
The cult quickly spread among the general public.
Its followers restored the temple
where the Enlightened used to worship the supreme gods.
The cults' priests promised freedom to the oppressed people.
and supported an armed uprising of the slaves.
In order to crush the unrest, the Empire sent a large fleet
under the command of General Herasim.
In response, the Highest Enlightened summoned the Ancients’ powers for help.
He sacrificed thousands of lives, spilling rivers of blood,
which opened the Rift between the worlds
Dormant volcanoes awakened, many islands went under water.
The Acribos were lost in darkness and chaos.
The Imperial troops suffered huge losses.
But General Herasim managed to break through to the cursed temple.
He annihilated the Highest Enlightened and sealed the Rift between the worlds.
The war was over. But the Acribian colony sustained great damage.
Celebrium shipments were stopped. Deprived of the much-needed energy source,
the Empire was gripped by a terrible crisis.
New expeditions were sent to the islands
but the Acribians destroyed whoever approached their lands.
Thousands of people were killed, never getting the chance to moor.
The Acribos became impregnable.
The Empire was crumbling, along with the hope to return to its former glory.
But there is always someone who can change history.
This time things will be different.
